speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Resources and Development) moved
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 339, to amend the National Housing Act, 1944.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as the house leader, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier), indicated last evening, it was my wish to be in Lunenburg today to attend the funeral of Senator William Duff, whose death followed that of Mrs. Duff by only seven weeks. Having regard to the amount of work which is still remaining, and the obvious desire of hon. members to conclude the business of the house at as early a date as possible, it was considered that I should remain in Ottawa

for this discussion on second reading of the bill to amend the National Housing Act.
All members who knew Senator Duff will appreciate how anxious I was to pay a final tribute to him by being in Lunenburg today. Among the many fine qualities possessed by my late good friend, however, was his great sense of responsibility, and under the circumstances I am sure it would have been his wish that I remain in Ottawa today to enable parliament to adhere to the program of business before it.
Before dealing with the amendments proposed for the National Housing Act I would like to make some remarks of a general nature.
During 1952 the number of housing starts increased steadily. For the year as a whole starts numbered about 84,000, excluding conversions, an increase of 21 per cent over the 68,600 of 1951. There were 93,000 houses started in 1950. In the last quarter of 1952 starts were taking place at a rate higher than the previous record rate of 1950.
Completions on the other hand declined in 1952 to 74,000 units, as compared with 81,000 in 1951. This decline reflects the much smaller carryover into 1952 of dwellings under construction than there were at the beginning of 1951. The carryover has been restored, as a result of the increase in housing starts in 1952, and we entered the year 1953 with 56,000 dwellings under construction. There is already, therefore, an auspicious prospect for completions in 1953. This high rate of building has continued this year. During the first quarter of 1953, dwellings started in centres of 5,000 population and over numbered 10,500. This represents an increase of 69 per cent over the same period in 1951, and as a matter of fact it has been the best first quarter on record from the point of view of the number of dwellings started in Canada.
The large number of houses that were brought under construction in the later part of 1952 may be attributed to a number of favourable factors on both the demand side and the supply side of the market. For one thing the demand for new houses was supported by a continued high level of net family formation. Not only was there a good increase in the number of families in 1952, but the families had more money with which to buy houses. Fortunately, our lending institutions showed an increased interest during 1952 in mortgage loans for new residential construction in general and for National Housing Act loans in particular.
Institutional loans for new residential construction were approved for 46,000 units in

1952, an increase of 19 per cent over 1951. Joint loans under the National Housing Act were approved for 27,488 dwellings in 1952, or 39 per cent more than in 1951. Had it not been for this increased flow of mortgage money, the rise in demand deriving from family formation and higher real incomes could not have been effective to the same extent. Brisk demand in 1952 was accompanied by favourable supply conditions. Except for cement in certain localities and some minor steel items, construction materials were readily available where and when needed. Even in regard to cement and steel, the situation improved towards the end of the year. We reaped the benefits of ample material supplies, not only in terms of a steady flow of production at the site, but also in terms of cost stability. During the course of 1952 the price of building materials for a house was about the same as in 1951. Neither was there any marked shortage of labour in 1952 for the residential work in hand despite an increase in other types of construction. However, wages in the construction field increased during the year by about 9 per cent.
Combined material cost and wage rates in construction were about 3 per cent higher in 1952 than in 1951; the prices of new houses increased even less. This is the smallest rise in construction costs that has occurred from one year to the next since the war. So much for the calendar year just past. What of the cumulative program over the past seven years, from the beginning of 1946 to December 31, 1952? In this period starts in Canada, excluding conversions of existing buildings, totalled 570,000.
I would now like to summarize the accomplishments of the federal government in the field of housing during this period and the extent to which the support and stimulus provided by the National Housing Act has resulted in such a large volume of new housing. During this period 141,294 dwelling units have received financial assistance under the joint loan terms of the National Housing Act. Another 30,000 units were built on direct government account. This included 28,000 units in the veterans' rental housing program and another 1,760 units under the public housing section 35 of the National Housing Act. In addition the rental insurance plan has accounted for about 18,000 units.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, from funds voted by parliament, has built about 12,000 permanent married quarters for the armed services. In addition, a modest number of units have been built for other government departments, including the
National Housing Act
Department of Defence Production. Housing assistance has also been provided by the federal government under the Veterans Land Act, the Canadian Farm Loan Act and the Farm Improvement Loans Act. All these activities, of which hon. members will note that joint loans compose much the largest element, have had the net effect that about two of every five permanent post-war houses in Canada have received stimulus or assistance of one kind or another from the federal government. In making this tally I have not taken into account the 11,000 temporary units made available under the emergency shelter regulations.
I would point out that apart from the direct construction to which I have referred this housing has been produced by supplementing the efforts of those agencies whose ordinary business it is to deal directly in new housing. We have supported the builders with guarantees, we have supported the lending institutions by joint participation in National Housing Act loans; during the immediate post-war years we ensured that materials flowed into the residential field. Generally, the policy was then, as it is now, for the federal government to give secondary help and assistance rather than to assume a primary role.
I would like to discuss for a few moments some of the provisions of the act and to lay emphasis upon those few sections which supplement the basic policy of the government to utilize to the utmost existing private mortgage outlets and other private agencies directly connected with the construction of houses.	.
It will be recalled that apart from the provision for direct government loans to limited dividend companies, the National Housing Act, passed in 1944, relied upon the initiative of private enterprise and old established institutions to use their facilities to provide new housing.
In June, 1947, section 31A was introduced. The difficulty had arisen that the lending institutions were unable or unwilling to make loans in outlying areas. The new section authorized Central Mortgage to make loans on the same terms to the borrowers as joint loans where such loans are not being made by lending institutions.
Since the introduction of section 31A its application has in practice been widened to cover three other types of housing. First, rental insurance projects for which private institutional mortgage loans are not available may qualify for direct corporation loans. Second, the 90 per cent loans available in respect of houses for defence workers are

National Housing Act
made on direct corporation account under this section. And third, since last July loans placed by lending institutions, acting as agents of the corporation, may be made on direct corporation account in centres of from about 5,000 to 50,000 population. Some of these centres were being deprived of mortgage money and the agency arrangement was conceived to prevent the withdrawal of National Housing Act benefits therefrom.
Under section 31A of the act net loans have been approved to the end of 1952 in respect of 16,290 dwellings. Of these, 13,030 were under the rental insurance plan, 1,848 were in areas outside the operations of lending institutions, 1,974 were in connection with 90 per cent loans for defence workers' housing, and 96 were under agency agreements.
Another change in the National Housing Act took place in June of 1948 with the introduction of the rental insurance plan. This was devised to establish incentives to promote the construction of more rental housing by builders. Under the plan the corporation is authorized to make certain guarantees in regard to new rental housing projects, in return for an agreed premium. To builders of approved projects the corporation guarantees a minimum gross annual rental. The amount of guaranteed rental itself is calculated as enough to pay all operating and financial costs and provide to the owner of the project a return of 2 per cent on his equity. As a condition of this guarantee the rental units come under a rental ceiling set by the corporation for a period of three years. By the end of 1952 the number of rental dwellings for which this type of guarantee has been approved was over 18,000.
During the post-war years the only important new supply of low rental housing was provided by the veterans' rental program. This had been achieved by arrangements, with the approval of provincial governments, between the federal government and the municipalities whereby a portion of the land and services was provided by the municipality and the construction was carried out by the federal government. By the middle of 1949 this program had come to a conclusion and at that time, by amendment to the National Housing Act, parliament authorized the government to enter the field of public housing through the medium of section 35. It was felt that a more permanent arrangement for providing housing, and particularly rental housing, was required for those whose needs could not be met by existing facilities of the National Housing Act. It was also considered that some positive action should be taken to assist in the solution of one of the most pressing

problems which had already beset the production of housing-that is, the lack of serviced land. Not only was section 35 designated to deal with these two problems, but it was also fitted into our federal structure of government by leaving initiative with the provincial governments so that arrangements with municipalities could take place through them.
Most provincial governments have responded by enacting legislation which enables them to work with the federal government in partnership, the general basis being that the federal government provides 75 per cent and the provincial governments 25 per cent of the funds required for work undertaken through section 35. The provincial governments are, of course, free to share their part of the costs with municipalities in whatever proportion they may see fit.
In the application of section 35 to low rental housing we have now established some basic principles of administration. The ownership of such low rental projects is vested in the federal-provincial partnership and a local housing authority is set up to manage the property.
It is the firm policy of the federal government that federal subsidies provided under section 35 of the act shall be made available only to families which need such assistance in housing. We believe that it is improper for the taxpayers as a whole to subsidize families who can afford to pay economic rentals or their equivalent in the home ownership field. In this respect our policy is similar to that of the United States.
In addition to the subsidized low rental projects, we have undertaken rental projects which do not involve any subsidy but produce a rent revenue sufficient to recover full costs of amortization, management and local taxes. The tenants eligible for this housing must have incomes not less than four and not more than six times the rent.
The land assembly operations under section 35 are quite distinct from those which involve the construction and ownership of rental projects, though they are based on the same ratio of federal-provincial financing and the same sharing of profits or losses. Here the financial resources of the federal government are available to assist municipalities in the preparing of land for residential use. We have so far undertaken with the provinces to acquire 24 tracts of land ranging in size from 10 acres to 500 acres which will yield 11,900 serviced house lots.
Mr. Speaker, I have reviewed some of the actions taken under the National Housing Act in order to give some background for

the amendments now being proposed. It will be clear to hon. members that the role of the federal government in this field is a complex one. The government must deal on the one hand as a mortgage banker in full co-operation with the financial institutions who have their own proper purposes. On the other hand we must deal in a co-operative spirit with provincial governments who have jurisdiction in the field of housing and who have widely differing traditions and attitudes in the matter of housing. And finally, the construction that results from our efforts is placed in the local community and must complement the present array of buildings there. Now it is a feature of the National Housing Act as originally introduced and frequently improved by parliament that it enables the lending of support by the federal government on behalf of the citizens of Canada to meet a wide variety of needs. I venture to say that in no federal state outside Canada is there found a more comprehensive, flexible and versatile instrument to help the people meet their need for shelter than has been passed by parliament.
I opened my remarks today with some observations on the housing program of 1952. The rising levels of starts and strong demand in 1953 will, I am sure, prove a source of gratification to all of us. But we are still faced with difficulties.
Most important among these I consider the shortage of serviced land. The post-war rate of housing starts has far exceeded the rate of lot development and the growth of municipal services, such as sewer, water, road and school facilities. Therefore the amount of available serviced land has rapidly diminished. In some centres substantial programs of new residential development must wait on the provision of additional serviced land, and in others a similar situation is approaching. An increasing proportion of current housebuilding requires the development of new land.
This problem has two important aspects, that of the municipality, and that of the house buyer. The problem of the municipality is more immediate. For the municipality, residential land development means the extension of pavements and existing utilities and commonly involves the provision of new schools. In some cases further land development may require enlarged central pumping plants and the like. In any case, such land development means heavy municipal expenditures. These expenditures must be financed by municipal borrowings. Because of unwillingness or inability to borrow, the municipalities do not always respond as soon as the
National Housing Act
need for additional serviced land arises. The financing problems are of particular severity in metropolitan environs where the growth associated with a great city is apt to be thrust upon a junior municipality which is predominantly residential, and which lacks those commercial and industrial assessments that bulk so large in the ordinary municipal tax base. It is this non-residential property that has traditionally given some relief to the home owner in paying for expensive urban services.
The development of serviced land under section 35 is providing financial relief to municipalities only in respect to the installation of facilities within the project. The municipality must still meet the costs of school construction, trunk main extensions and the expansion of central municipality plant.
As that problem is solved and serviced land is made ready in greater quantities, it may be necessary to stimulate a corresponding increase in the flow of mortgage money. The introduction of the agency arrangement in 1952, by which the corporation extended the direct loan facilities of section 31A to cities of from 5,000 to 50,000 population, is already a step in that direction.
Life and fire insurance companies, trust and loan companies and fraternal societies are the main source of private mortgage money for new houses in Canada. These institutions have played a most important role in financing house construction. Their participation in the mortgage lending field increased from 1951 to 1952. Commitments in the whole mortgage field in 1951 amounted to $434 million and in 1952 to $497 million, an increase of 15 per cent. The increase of commitment in the residential field is even greater. I mention these figures because I would like to consider them in relation to the whole investment operation carried out by these companies. The level of net mortgage investment by these companies in 1952 absorbed about half of their total increase in assets during the year. Their mortgage holdings at the end of the year represented something more than one-quarter of their total assets. Present levels of institutional mortgage investment indicate that lending institutions wish not just to maintain but to increase the relative importance of their mortgage portfolios.
Now to deal more directly with the terms of the bill before the house:	The first
amendment vests in approved lending institutions the power to act in an agency capacity on behalf of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This is accomplished by adding

National Housing Act
paragraph (c) to subsection X of section 3 of the present statute. That section provides that notwithstanding limitations that may be contained in other legislation, an approved lending institution shall have power to make loans in accord with and in the proportions mentioned in the National Housing Act. In this connection hon. members will recall that the Insurance Act normally limits mortgage lending by insurance companies to 60 per cent of the lending value whereas under the National Housing Act this is increased to 80 per cent by government participation. The section in addition authorizes lending companies to purchase mortgages from Central Mortgage. No change is made in these particulars. The new clause authorizes the agency provisions. It is being included by way of abundant caution. We felt that the present legislation is adequate but while lending institutions believe that they have the power to act as the agent of the corporation, they indicated that they would feel more secure if there was an express empowering provision in the National Housing Act.
As hon. members are aware, under section 31A of the National Housing Act the corporation makes loans on its own account on terms similar to joint loans in communities of about 5,000 and less. Lending institutions have been servicing the larger centres of population. Last year, however, when mortgage money did not appear to be available to give full coverage of all areas in Canada, the corporation was authorized by the government to make an arrangement with lending institutions by which they could make loans in areas up to 50,000, with the funds being provided by Central Mortgage. Under the arrangement the companies administer the loans for the first two years, during which time they have an option under which they can purchase a three-quarters interest in the loan, thus reconstituting it as a joint loan. At the present time five companies have signed the agency agreement, and up to the end of the year ninety-six loans had been approved.
Another provision in the bill empowers the corporation on its own account to make supplementary loans for borrowers' charges. Under the statute, where there is a joint loan in existence the company and the corporation together may make a supplementary loan to a borrower for the purpose of protecting the mortgage security. It would be helpful if the corporation had the same power in respect of direct corporation loans to meet emergency cases that might arise. As an example, there might be a failure of a central heating plant in a large housing development financed by the corporation after

a period of years and the owners might not be in a position to finance the installation of a new plant. This would mean that the project would not be rentable. In order to put the project in a position to operate, the corporation could finance by way of supplementary loan the cost of such installation. While we do not look forward to cases of this kind arising, it is considered that the corporation should have such authority.
Parliament is being asked to amend the section in the National Housing Act that established the integrated housing plan. As hon. members know, under these provisions in the act the corporation is authorized to enter into contracts with builders to encourage the construction of houses for sale to veterans. The existing legislation provides that such contracts shall require the builder to finance the construction of the houses under the provisions of the National Housing Act and to offer the houses so built for sale at a price not exceeding the price fixed in the contract with Central Mortgage. The section further provides that the corporation shall agree to purchase from the builder any house that he is unable to sell on the market. It is now proposed that in return for the corporation's undertaking to repurchase a house, the builder should pay a premium at a rate to be established by the governor in council. It is proposed further to amend the integrated housing section by enlarging the class of persons to whom houses can be offered in the first instance by builders to include defence workers as well as veterans.
The arrangement is that for a certain period after the completion of the house the builder cannot consider any applications other than those of veterans and defence workers. After the expiration of this specified period the house may be offered on the market at or below the fixed price. If he is unable to sell it within a certain period the builder may then require the corporation to take the house off his hands.
Then, too, there are revisions of the sections which provide for the cumulative statutory votes. For home ownership loans and losses under the previous housing acts and the existing act an increase is sought from $300 million to $500 million, while the cumulative total requested for rental housing loans is $250 million, instead of the present $150 million.
The rent control period for rental insurance projects in the present legislation is being dealt with. The amount of rent that may be charged by a borrower in respect of each unit of a project financed under the rental

insurance plan is limited by an agreement between the corporation and the borrower.
Under the present legislation the period of control, which is three years, runs from the date of completion of the entire project. The provision has worked a hardship in the case of very large projects in which the completion dates for the various units may extend over a period of years. The new legislation would permit the rent control period to be on a unit basis. Administratively, it will be dealt with by groups of units.
The bill contains a revision of the rehousing, sometimes referred to as slum clearance, provisions of the National Housing Act. Section 12 of the act provides for federal grants to a municipality to assist in clearing, replanning, rehabilitating and modernizing slum areas or blighted or substandard areas.
As it presently reads, section 12 authorizes the minister, with the approval of the governor in council, to make a grant to a municipality to assist it to acquire and clear a slum area. It is a condition of the grant under the present legislation that the area which is acquired and cleared be sold to a limited-dividend housing company for the construction of a housing project under section 9 of the act, or to a life insurance company for the construction of a housing project under section 11. As hon. members know, section 9 provides for loans for low rent housing, and section 11 authorizes lending companies to proceed with the construction and operation of low and moderate rental housing.
At present the amount of the grant must not exceed one-half the difference between the cost of the acquisition and clearance of the land and the price at which it is sold to a limited-dividend company or a life insurance company. The remainder of the excess costs must be borne by the municipality or by the province and the municipality jointly. The proposed amendment provides that in addition to the possible Sale of the land to a limited-dividend company or a life insurance company it may also be sold to a province and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation jointly for a housing development under section 35 of the National Housing Act. This is in accordance with the recommendation of the standing committee on banking and commerce after it completed its study of the annual report of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation last year. The basis of sharing the costs of acquisition and clearance will remain unchanged. The cost of the future development under section 35 will be borne 25 per cent by the province and 75 per cent by the federal government. The present legislation requires that the cleared
National Housing Act
area be redeveloped for housing purposes. The proposed amendments will permit the cleared area to be used either for housing purposes or for a municipal, provincial or federal public purpose, provided that the municipality makes available for a housing development an alternative area of a size sufficient to house at least the same number of persons as were living in the cleared area. The provision relating to the use of an alternative area will apply only where the slum area to be cleared is designated on the municipal plan for use ultimately for public purposes.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to explain that part II of the bill comprising sections 8 to 15 constitutes a rewrite of sections 1 to 7. As hon. members know, the Revised1 Statutes of Canada, 1952, are presently on the press. Part II has reference to the revised National Housing Act.

Mr. Speaker, it is evident, both from the terms of Bill 339, and from the interesting statement just made to the house by the minister, that we are dealing with a bill of limited objectives and limited extent. Indeed, contrary to the expectations of some hon. members, the bill does not seem to go much beyond the terms of the resolution debated in the house on April 21.
Sir, I am sure there will be no question as to the desire of the house to give full support to the bill, limited as its objectives may be. Indeed, it may be said that at no time has parliament hesitated when called upon to enact housing legislation in any form which would be of assistance in meeting this great and still pressing problem.
Similarly, when questions have arisen-and I refer to the entire post-war period-as to making greater sums of money available from the consolidated revenue fund for the assistance of housing, and to implement sound schemes, there has never been any hesitation on the part of parliament to provide what was required. Therefore it may be assumed that while the bill may not go as far in its objectives as some may have hoped, nevertheless to the extent that it does attempt to improve our housing legislation it will, I am sure, have the support of hon. members.
The minister said less than I had hoped he would say concerning the need for housing in Canada. There are some arresting figures on this subject which I suggest should be considered by the house. Speaking in the debate on the resolution last Tuesday, as reported at page 4153 of Hansard, I drew attention to definite figures which had been

National Housing Act
placed a year ago before the standing committee on banking and commerce in its very extensive and, I think, helpful review of the housing problem, and the administration of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
The figures for the first complete six postwar years, namely the years 1946 to 1951, inclusive, showed that in that period new housing units completed in all Canada numbered 495,887, whereas during the same period net family formations totalled 513,000. Therefore in that six-year period family formations in Canada had exceeded the number of housing units constructed in this country to the extent of 17,113 units. We have not been furnished with the complete figures for 1952.
However, on reference to the last quarterly report issued by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, in the publication entitled "Housing in Canada" we read in the opening paragraph, dealing with the fourth quarter of 1952:
Net family formation in Canada during the first three-quarters of 1952, at 67,000, continued close to the 1951 rate. Slightly more than one-quarter of this was attributable to immigration, as indicated by net migration of married females into Canada.
Well, if the rate of family formations in the last three months of the year 1952 even approximates the rate for the first nine months of that year, then it is quite evident that the number of family formations in Canada in 1952 must have come very close to the figure of 85,000 or 90,000.
Now, what was our record in house construction in Canada in 1952? The minister has said this morning that the number of completions in Canada in 1952 was 74,000. It is evident therefore that, even with what the minister has said about the accomplishments in that year, again in our rate of housing construction we have fallen behind the rate of net family formations in Canada; and instead of making any dent in the backlog of housing needs in Canada it is evident, on the contrary, that the backlog did actually increase in 1952.
We will all be gratified to find that there were at least 74,000 houses built in Canada, and that in the first three months of 1953 the number of starts has shown an encouraging rate. We will all be pleased at that. But let us not close our eyes to the other side of the problem. Let us not put on blinkers and simply consider the rate of construction. Let us see the problem as a whole and in doing so realize that even in the face of these figures house construction in Canada in 1952 once again fell behind the rate of net family formations and now for a period of seven years from 1946 to 1952 inclusive we

have added to the backlog of housing needs in Canada instead of reducing it.
While Canadians are increasing in numbers and marrying at continued high rates, immigration in 1952 added a total of 164,498 persons to the population. While this figure represents a reduction of 30,000 when compared with the number of immigrants coming into the country in 1951, nevertheless it is a substantial number of people for whom to find homes. Therefore we cannot sit back and view with any degree of satisfaction the housing picture in Canada today or the efforts that are being made to meet the needs.
The fact of the matter is that the problem is very great and very critical. One looked with disappointment this morning at the statement of government housing policy for some clear recognition of the still critical nature of the housing problem in Canada. Emphasis was on accomplishment. Whatever may be said for accomplishment, the fact is that it was not enough to meet current needs. There must be a much more realistic approach to this problem. There must be a greater sense of urgency in our approach to it.
An eminent businessman in Toronto, Mr. C. L. Burton, reviewing a long and active life, wrote a book last year entitled "A Sense of Urgency". If I could sum up the shortcomings in tne government's position with respect to housing in Canada it would be this:	There is on the part of the government a lack of a sense of urgency with respect to the problem.
When the minister draws attention to the completion last year of 74,000 housing units in Canada, a reduction of 7,000 as compared with 1951, but marked, it is true, toy an increase in the rate of construction in the later months of 1952 which was carried forward into the earlier months of 1953 as compared with the previous year, let us be frank in recognizing that the decline in housing construction that set in in the late spring of 1951 and continued at quite an alarming rate throughout the balance of 1951 and into 1952 was in large measure the result of deliberate government policy. The curbs which the government placed on housing construction in 1951 had their inevitable effect in reducing the rate of construction of needed homes in Canada and the effects were felt for at least a year. When we see house construction in Canada reversing its trend in the latter part of 1952 we are seeing the house-building industry overcoming those barriers which were created by deliberate government policy in the spring of 1951.

There are some trends that are becoming evident in Canada in relation to the housing problem which should be taken into account by those who are devising housing policy in Canada. I draw attention to several recent government reports which I think will command high interest on the part of the house.
The dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin of March 17, 1953, draws attention to a substantial increase in the decade 1941-51 in the percentage of Canadian dwellings occupied by owners. The note reads:
Home ownership made a big advance in Canada during the ten years from 1941 to 1951, according to a census bulletin on housing by tenure and type of dwelling published by the dominion bureau of statistics.
Of the 3,409,295 occupied dwellings in Canada's 10 provinces in 1951, 2,236,955 or 65-6 per cent were occupied by owners and the remaining 1,172,340 or 34-4 per cent by tenants. This represents a substantial jump in both the number and percentage of owner-occupied dwellings over 1941.
The report then proceeds to give figures with respect to the various provinces.
The next trend to which attention is drawn is indicated in the daily bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics of March 19. Reference is made here to the trend toward three to five-room dwellings as indicated by the 1951 census results. The note reads:
A trend towards three to five room dwellings in preference to dwellings of larger or smaller sizes is indicated in a 1951 census bulletin on dwelling size published by the dominion bureau of statistics. Comparison of 1941 and 1951 figures for the nine older provinces reveals that in the decade three to five rooms supplanted six or more rooms as the predominant size range, and accounted for 49-6 per cent of all dwellings at the time of the last census as compared with 43-3 per cent in 1941. At the same time, the proportion of dwellings with six or more rooms dropped to 43-6 per cent from 48-3 per cent, while dwellings with one or two rooms represented only 6-8 per cent of the total in 1951 against 8-4 per cent ten years earlier.
The third trend to which attention is drawn may in part be the natural consequence of the first trend which I mentioned, namely, the trend toward an increase in the percentage of owner-occupied homes in Canada. This trend is referred to in the daily bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics of April 16. It is headed "Larger Percentage of Owned Dwellings with Both First and Second Mortgages" and reads:
A larger proportion of Canada's owner-occupied homes had both first and second mortgages in 1951 than in 1941, but a smaller percentage had only a first mortgage, according to a 1951 census bulletin on rents and mortgages published by the dominion bureau of statistics.
Of the 1,654,045 owner-occupied non-farm dwellings in the 10 provinces in 1951, 1,137,040 or 68-7 per cent reported no mortgage, 478,740 or 29 per cent reported a first mortgage only, and 38,265 or 2-3 per cent reported both first and second mortgages. In 1941, 607,669 or 68-8 per cent of the 883,294
National Housing Act
dwellings in the nine provinces had no mortgage, 263,390 or 29-8 per cent had a first mortgage only, and 12,233 or 1-4 per cent had both first and second mortgages.
These trends no doubt have been evident in some degree or other to all hon. members, although the trends are by no means uniform in the different parts of Canada. But it is evident that serious account must be taken of trends in this post-war period as reported in the 1951 census figures and as compared with 1941. We have made some headway in the direction of increasing the proportion of owner-occupied houses in Canada and to the extent to which part I of the National Housing Act has assisted in that direction it certainly deserves the continued support of all parties in this house-and it has received the support of all parties from the outset.
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to review all of the factors that are evident today and which have a direct bearing on what we may fairly expect by way of house construction in Canada. I reviewed those in my remarks in the house on April 21 in the debate at the resolution stage. I do not propose to repeat them, but the minister in his statement this morning mentioned, as I think I did in my remarks a week ago, that no longer is there a shortage of labour retarding house construction in Canada. Happily, house construction is not being retarded today by any shortage of labour; and, in the second place, house construction in Canada today is not being retarded by any shortage of building materials. In the third place, it is evident that prices at the moment at any rate show some indication of stability, as Mr. Mansur described in a recent speech.
Houses that might have been built in 1951, and which were not built because of the errors in government policy at that time, could have been built at lower cost than houses can be built today. In July last the economic research department of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, in its annual review of mortgage lending in Canada, drew attention to the fact that in 1951 it cost Canadians $10,211 to buy a house and that a down payment of $3,188 was required. Those figures immediately invite comparison with the year 1950. The average dwelling cost that I have mentioned represented an increase of 16 per cent over the 1950 average cost of a dwelling, which was $8,805. The down payments also greatly increased. The 1951 requirement, as I have mentioned, was $3,188. The figure for down payments in 1950, as disclosed in this survey, was $1,928. The increase in the down payment required on the part of Canadians purchasing homes in 1951 over that

National Housing Act
required by those purchasing them in 1950 was 65 per cent. Now, Mr. Speaker, no one can overlook the significance of those figures. They do emphasize the responsibility that the government must bear for policies which they applied and which had the effect of retarding house construction two years ago when construction costs were substantially lower than they are now, and' when houses could be purchased with an average down payment very substantially lower than the down payment required today.
In my remarks a week ago I drew attention to the fact that we have entered a period now when we must distinguish, as Mr. Mansur very fairly pointed out in his testimony before the banking and commerce committee last June, between housing demand and housing need. When speaking of housing demand we are referring to the effective housing demand on the part of those who have the economic means to acquire the needed housing where housing is physically available. Housing need must be measured in wider terms to include housing needs of many who have not the economic resources to satisfy their housing needs today. This problem becomes more acute as the need for larger down payments increases and as the cost of house construction rises.
Now, sir, the bill that the minister has introduced has as one of its more conspicuous features amendments to section 12 of the act, directly related to section 35, designed in effect, as it has been described, to "marry" more closely the operations of section 12 and 35. As the minister has said, these amendments were proposed in the report of the banking and commerce committee to the house around July 1 last year, and I am glad that the minister has seen fit to bring forward legislation to carry those proposals into effect. Section 35 was enacted by parliament in November, 1949, with very high hopes. The government was not at all diffident in the claims it then put forward for the accomplishments that might be expected from this legislative child of the government. They conjured up pictures of great steps being taken to build development schemes and housing projects which were going to have the effect of meeting the housing needs of those who were not in a position to supply their own immediate housing requirements. Well, Mr. Speaker, after three and a half years of experience with section 35 the fact of the matter is-whether because of the nature of the scheme embodied in section 35 or because the government has not put sufficient energy and drive behind the scheme-

the accomplishments to date have been disappointing.
If one turns to page 53 of the publication to which I made reference earlier, the "Housing in Canada" publication of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the fourth quarter of 1952, one will see that up to the end of September, 1952, the number of projects approved under section 35 for which contracts had been awarded totalled only 20. There was one in 1950; three in 1951; and the balance, namely 16, were in the first nine months of 1952. The total after almost three years of operation is 20 projects for which contracts have been awarded.
Let us also examine the figures for the number of dwellings involved. Up to September 30, 1952, the number of dwellings for which contracts have been awarded was 1,737; the number started was 1,322; and the number completed 371. It is not a record that will fill any hon. member or anyone who knows the housing needs of this country- particularly in and around the great metropolitan areas where today growth is so rapid- with any degree of satisfaction. They are very disappointing figures. One may express the hope, Mr. Speaker, that the amendments in this particular bill by which an attempt is made to marry the legislative effect of sections 12 and 35 will be more efficacious for the intended purpose than section 35 has been thus far. The scheme of section 35, let us admit it, is clumsy. It is clumsy because it involves the three levels of government. There may be some improvement in that regard in the amendment in the bill now before the house. There will be an opportunity to make further comment on that, Mr. Speaker, when we are in committee of the whole on the bill. It is a departure now to have provision being made by statute for contracts between the federal and municipal governments directly. It is true that the approval of the provincial government is required, but nevertheless it is evident that we are entering a period during which contracts may be entered into directly for, it is true, limited purposes between the federal and municipal governments. This may help to short-circuit some of the procedures and eliminate some of the delays, some of the cumbersome machinery which have deprived section 35 of the effect parliament intended it should have when it legislated that section in 1935.
There was not a word in the minister's statement today to indicate recognition of the necessity of some major step to meet the financial needs of the municipalities if we are to grapple effectively with the housing problem. In his statement the minister did

recognize that a major factor retarding house construction in Canada today is the shortage of serviced land, particularly in those areas immediately adjacent to the great metropolitan centres where the growth of population has been so very rapid. But how are we to cope with the problem confronting such municipalities? It is going to take a great deal more than enabling legislation of the kind we have before us to equip municipal governments to render effective assistance for this housing problem in the areas where the problem is so acute. These municipalities, Mr. Speaker, simply have not the means today to provide serviced land. Many of them are taking open steps to discourage house construction within their borders because they are unable to cope with the problems created by house construction and the extension of the burden upon the already heavily-laden taxpayer as the result of providing the needed services which the municipalities are required to provide. The cost of these services has risen by leaps and bounds. Look at the increases in the costs of construction of schools. They have simply skyrocketed. These are problems that are weighing upon the shoulders of the municipalities today with a greater burden than ever before in our history.
These municipalities are carrying on with the same limited tax base that they were given over 80 years ago. This limited tax base is completely unequal to the task of meeting the needs that are being placed upon municipalities today, particularly in areas of the type I have mentioned, as a result of the acute housing shortages. Not a word has been forthcoming from the government as to any policy of seeking the solution that must be found to a problem of that kind. We in this quarter of the house, Mr. Speaker, have said we are prepared to offer a policy in that regard. We propose that the dominion and the provinces sit down together to study the whole field of tax resources and work out an agreement by which there will be assured to the provincial governments, and through them to the municipal governments, adequate sources of tax revenue to meet the needs that are being placed upon the shoulders of the municipalities today. You will not cope effectively with the housing problem in Canada today, particularly in the areas where it is being most acutely felt, unless you take steps of the kind I have advocated to provide the municipalities with means adequate to discharge their responsibilities in relation to housing and the other needs.
I say to the minister, with all candour, that I think he is the best minister whom the government has placed in charge of the
National Housing Act
housing problem. In this post-war period we have had a succession of ministers to deal with it. I am going to say to the house that I think the present minister is the best of them. He has approached his duties in this house with a greater degree of frankness and candour, and I think conscientiousness also, than his predecessors. But as I have sought to point out, Mr. Speaker, there still is lacking on the part of the government that recognition of the urgency of this problem which must be the beginning of any serious attempt to meet it in all its harsh realities. In the second place, there is still manifest on the part of the government a lack of drive behind the efforts being made to meet the housing needs. There is too clear evidence of the fact that the government is content to count up the number of houses which have been built and to take satisfaction out of it; to stop there, without examining the rate at which the need has been outrunning our rate of house construction in Canada.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, there has not been on the part of the government that recognition of the necessity of assisting the municipalities, without which there will be no effective solution of the urgent housing problem in Canada.

My
criticism of the bill before us, Mr. Speaker, is that, as a bit of patchwork of tinkering with the National Housing Act, it has some merit. But it does not touch the root of our housing problem. When speaking during the resolution stage of this matter on April 24, I pointed out that, although the government has been negotiating with the finance companies and the real estate companies ever since the war, it has not yet evolved a housing policy that has met the situation.
The facts, as I pointed out, are that the backlog of housing that existed at the end of the war still exists and has increased. Competent authorities today assure us that there is a backlog of approximately 700,000 houses needed in Canada. We have been building at the rate of some 80,000 houses a year, which rate has fallen short of the number of newly-formed families in Canada so that we have not met the new need for houses each year. We have not touched the backlog that existed at the end of the war. If we are to catch up with that backlog within the next ten years-I would say that in a period of prosperity such as we have in Canada at the present time we should make every effort to catch up on that backlog- it would seem to me that we should plan our housing policy to catch up on that backlog within at least the next ten years. At that rate we must build at least 70,000 houses a year more than is required to fill the current

National Housing Act
need; in other words, to meet the need created by newly-formed families, provided they do not increase in future years but remain as they have been during the past two years. To catch up with that backlog, we should have a housing program that calls for at least 150,000 houses a year; that is,
70,000	if we are to catch up on that backlog within the next ten years and another 80,000 to take care of the increase required year by year by reason of the newly-formed families.
In this bill there is nothing to indicate that the present policy of the government will achieve that result. There is nothing to indicate that it will achieve it in the coming years any more than it has achieved it in the years immediately behind us. There are certain problems which have to be faced. The first of these is that the cost of building today-the cost of homes-has passed beyond the reach of tens of thousands of people who need homes. I think that is the first fact we must face. No matter how much money you put into the pool for finance companies to lend, tens of thousands of people who need homes today cannot afford to buy them or to rent them at today's prices. There is today a shortage of rental houses at prices at which tens of thousands of people, whose means will not allow them to buy homes, can rent; and there is nothing in this legislation which, to my mind, will adequately meet that difficulty.
Today other tens of thousands of people who have purchased homes in the past are over-burdened with mortgages which they have assumed. They are carrying these mortgages on a dangerously close margin. With any change in our present prosperity rate, with the slightest recession, thousands of these people are going to find themselves in difficulty in making the payments of principal and paying the interest on these mortgages which they have assumed. If we are to continue expecting people to buy homes at today's prices and to assume mortgages which probably it will be beyond their capacity to carry, we are not touching the root of the housing problem.
It is all very well to call a dominion-provincial conference, to get together with governments at other levels and to find out to what extent the federal government can come to the assistance of these municipalities or the provinces. But unless that conference meets for the express purpose of doing something about reducing the cost of housing and the carrying charges on housing, we shall not meet the situation.
First of all, we must give some consideration to a reduction in the interest rate that is being charged in connection with houses.

The minister tells us that this new amendment to the National Housing Act will make lending companies agents of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Again and again in this house within the past few years I have stated that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is nothing more or less than an agent of the lending companies. The basic difficulty in connection with the housing problem in the past has been that the government-in its anxiety to bolster capitalist enterprise, to maintain the position of the lending companies, and to look after the interests of the real estate companies- has been overlooking the needs of the common people of this country and has been placing the interests of these lending companies and corporations ahead of those of the people.
It is not a question of making these lending companies the agents of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation already is-and has been since its inception-the agent of the lending companies in this country. Every move that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has made down through the years has been made with the interests of these lending companies in mind and has been made in order to bolster the position of these companies and to see that their security is maintained. The fact that the cost of housing has passed beyond the reach of tens of thousands of Canadian citizens who need homes has not influenced the government's policy.
Today one of the first problems we must seek to tackle is that of a reduction in that interest rate of 5J per cent which these corporations today collect on their mortgages, subsidized as they are by the government; and that 5| per cent is too high for ordinary working-class people to carry. Today this government is subsidizing the steel industry and the gold industry. It is handing out subsidies right and left to capitalist enterprise. It is time that this government gave more consideration to subsidizing the needs of the people of Canada. We can subsidize housing just as well as we can subsidize the steel industry, the mining industry or other industries of a like nature in this country. In our opinion the government, through the Bank of Canada, should make loans directly to the builders at an interest rate of not more than 2 per cent. Until you can bring that interest rate down to that figure, tens of thousands of people in this country will not be able to buy homes.
In my speech on April 21 I pointed out that, in reducing the carrying charges on a home, a reduction in the interest rate can be

much more effective than a reduction in either material or labour costs. The great burden that rests upon the people of this country in the matter of housing is there in that 5J per cent interest rate that they have to pay. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that any government policy that aims to meet the needs of the people will use the facilities of the Bank of Canada to provide builders with loans at an interest rate of 2 per cent. Do that, and you will have solved most of the difficulties in the way of providing housing.
I have said that the government of today subsidizes a great many interests in this country. I am convinced, as is this group, that if those who cannot afford to buy houses but must rent are to have houses available, then the government must subsidize public housing authorities in order that rents may be brought more in line with the financial means of those low income dwellers.
Section 35 of the National Housing Act has not been working very effectively, and the present amendment seeks to bring section 12 and section 35 together to see if we cannot get more action through these public housing authorities. Not until the federal government assumes the responsibility of lending money directly to these public housing authorities will you find section 35 working satisfactorily. Do that, get away from the shackles of the finance companies, and use the facilities of this country to benefit the people of the country, and you will solve the housing problem.
Another basic shortcoming of the present policy is again the fact that this government, in their anxiety to boast of private, capitalist enterprise, are reluctant to go directly into the construction of houses. If you want to solve the housing problem, lend directly to the builders at interest rates of not more than 2 per cent, and use the facilities of the Bank of Canada to do that. Subsidize public housing authorities.
Some provision will have to be made whereby municipalities will get assistance from the federal government for the provision of schools and other facilities required by new housing developments.
In the third place, I submit that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation must go directly into the construction of low rental housing. It must build these houses and sell them or rent them at cost to the people who need them. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as this amendment to the National Housing Act, in my opinion, falls far short of what is necessary to meet our housing situation, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight):
That the said bill be not now read the second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of
National Housing Act
this house consideration should be given to the introducing of legislation to amend the National Housing Act, 1944, to permit:
(1)	Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to issue loans directly to the builder at an interest rate of 2 per cent;
(2)	Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to subsidize public housing authorities in order that rents may be brought into line with the financial means of low-income dwellers;
(3)	Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to enter the field of housing construction to build low-rental housing projects where such projects are needed but are not being constructed.
I am satisfied that if the government is prepared completely to overhaul their policy and the National Housing Act, as I have suggested, we shall meet our housing problem and we shall have no difficulty in overcoming the backlog of 700,000 houses within the next ten years and building enough houses to provide homes for the new-formed families of Canada. In other words, to build the
150,000	houses each year within the next ten years we shall have to overhaul drastically the National Housing Act.

I had intended to say something on this measure when it was in the resolution stage, but we were urged to wait until the bill came down so that we could examine it and know its details.
There are a number of questions that should be asked in respect of the general situation existing with the home owners of Canada. I have reference to the tremendous amount of debt which must exist in respect of housing if we look at it as a whole. I do believe of course that we would not have the houses that we have today, even if there still is a shortage, had it not been for the fact that our people have been able to borrow money in order to build. I suppose that a great majority of home owners today would never have been able to own their homes had they not been able to secure some financial assistance somewhere, and when they first bought their homes undoubtedly they were mortgaged.
I do believe it would be rather an alarming picture if we were to get the entire scene as it relates to the total housing debt. I do not mean simply by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation; I mean if we could get something from the bureau of statistics relating to the amount of total debt that is actually owed today by those who are buying their homes.
I believe that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have in a measure been able to assist people to acquire their homes. But I am in agreement with the previous speaker that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to a great extent has been a

National Housing Act
government agency acting as a sort of watchdog for the security of the lending institutions. I am not saying that in a spirit of undue or harsh criticism. However, I think all hon. members will agree that what is needed is some action which will enable those of low income to purchase their own homes. That can be done only by offering them low initial payments, in the first instance. I am not opposed to the procedure of borrowing on homes. As I have said before, most people would not own their homes if they had not had the opportunity of borrowing money in the first instance. However, there are vast numbers of young married people who are now starting out in life-and perhaps some older people, too-who are in the lower income brackets, who are paying rent, sometimes high rent which takes up a great proportion of their income. These are people in the lower income brackets who could not possibly begin to build houses because they have not sufficient money to make the initial payments.
Let us analyse this matter from the personal point of view. Let us suppose for the moment that hon. members are in the low income bracket. Let us suppose that we are receiving only a couple of hundred dollars each month. Today that is considered a low income. We will suppose that we have no insurance on which we can borrow and no friends who will come to our assistance. Perhaps our friends, too, are in the low income brackets. How is a person in that position going to get $2,000 or $3,000 as a first payment on a home? How are we going to acquire enough money even to buy a lot? It is almost an impossibility.
It does seem to me that something should be done to enable people in the lower income brackets to commence buying their homes. I agree with the hon. member who preceded me in the statement that there could be a national housing act that would enable home owners to borrow money at a very low rate of interest. After all, I fancy the bulk of mortgage money comes from the lending institutions. If there is any expansion of credit going on at all, that expansion is brought about by the process of creating money out of nothing. That is still the position we take, a position that cannot be denied. And if an interest rate of more than 5 or 5J per cent is demanded it creates a tremendous burden of interest debt. In my view the interest should be only a fraction more than the small amount required for the administration of the lending institutions.
I should like to ask the minister four questions on the general subject of housing. I do not ask these questions with particular

reference to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. They are directed, rather, to the entire housing situation in Canada, whether the building of a home is through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or through some other method of borrowing.
My first question is this: How many home owners in Canada today have clear titles to their homes?
My second question is this: How many people in Canada have bought homes and are still paying for them?
My third question is this: What is the total amount of mortgages or debts held against the total number of home owners?
My fourth question is this: What is the average debt on each home?
The answers to these questions would be most helpful and revealing. I cannot help believing that, should there be a business recession or slump, or a period of unemployment, houses would be available for a song. People would lose their equities in their homes. A home owner wants to hang on to his home as long as possible. However, we know what happens in a time of depression: When the depression strikes, people begin to move around the country. They say, "Well, there may be an opportunity for us somewhere else. Let us sell, and move." No one knows where they go. The recession is on, there is a deflation in prices, and the people lose their equities in their homes.
I hate to think what would happen if we had another recession. It would be alarming even to imagine what would happen to the home owners of Canada if a business recession should take place. It is understood that those of us in this part of the house believe in private enterprise. We believe that people should be free to build or to buy their own home as they choose. We believe that, if there is any government agency at all, it should be designed to assist citizens in the building of their homes.
Then, there is another matter connected with the bill to which I would direct the attention of the house. Whether others have detected it or not, I cannot say, but in the bill there is a somewhat modified provision for slum clearance. I am sure all would say that that is a good feature, and I would agree. But the principle I would bring before the house is this: Why should there ever have been any slums? What creates slum conditions? As I have been pausing and musing in consideration of this matter I have thought it wise to consult the dictionary to find out the exact meaning of the word "slum".

The Concise Oxford Dictionary gives the following definition:
Dirty back street or court or alley in city. To go about the slums, to visit or examine conditions of inhabitants; hence slummer.
Unless we get down to brass tacks we are always going to have these problems before us. Does it not occur to the minister and to the government that the reason we have to talk about slum clearance is not simply that certain sections of the city have become old and should be brought up to date or that certain buildings should be pulled down? It goes deeper than that. Everything grows old; we grow old; buildings grow old; railroads grows old.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Governments grow old.

Governments grow old, that goes without saying. But it goes deeper than that. The reason there are slums, the reason there are dirty back streets, the reason we have to examine into the condition of the inhabitants of certain areas is that governments in the past have not adopted policies that would give the people a proper income so they could live decently. That is the deeper aspect of this situation.
All we have to do is to ask ourselves what is the reason that we have slums. Have we building materials to build extensively in order to give people decent places in which to live? Of course we have building materials. Is there a lack of timber? We have forests galore in Canada. Is there a lack of cement? We have all the cement in Canada or materials to make it that is required. Have we unskilled labour? I think we have plenty of labour. What is wrong then? We have all the materials, we have the ability to do it, but the people just have not enough money.

Everybody's fault but yours.
Nlr. Hansell: I think that one almost has to assume that attitude when he is debating in this house. We all think we are right, we all think we have an argument, we all want to solve the problems of the day. We are now discussing housing problems. I say that it goes far deeper than just meets the eye. Governments have been in power and slum conditions have developed in this country.
And right in Alberta.
Of course they are right in Alberta because there are people with low incomes there as well as in other parts of the country.

And lots of federal taxation.

The whole financial policy of this country, which is the responsibility of this government, is what keeps people on low income no matter where they live. There is no question about that; there is no argument about that. It is really a shame that governments have to talk about slum clearance. For a government to have to put that in a bill is just an indictment that they have failed in their policies. There is no argument about that. You have to look deeper for the reason.
The reason is that the financial policy pursued, which is built upon debt and taxation, is one that will strangle the economic life out of our people. It is all right for us to say that we are living in a period of prosperity, but anyone who knows anything about busts and booms knows full well that when we are living in a period that people call prosperous, it is a false prosperity because it is built on debt. That is the responsibility of this government because it is this government that has the responsibility for currency, credit and banking.
I notice it is nearly one o'clock but perhaps I might say just a few words in closing. I have a number of other things that I should like to discuss, but perhaps I can do that when we are in committee. We may be entering a period of nominal peace. In his speech the other day President Eisenhower said that if the soviet were sincere in their shift of policy a good deal of the money now spent on defence could be diverted to other purposes. He gave a number of illustrations which were rather alarming to me. One was that the cost of one modern bomber would house 80,000 people.
That is an alarming thing. We should have a citizenry in Canada with incomes sufficiently high so that they can provide themselves with homes, with nice grounds and everything well painted. Then we shall be a respectable nation. I am not blaming the minister, because the minister is himself a victim of the financial policy which the government is pursuing.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as Your Honour has pointed out, this amendment was drafted in the light of the right that is set out in citation 657 of Beauchesne's third edition. As has been indicated frequently, there seems to be some ambiguity as to what the citation means, but it does seem to me that it provides for just such a proposition as is contained in the amendment moved by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy). Let me read citation 657:
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy or provisions of the bill-
Perhaps I might interject at that point that is exactly what my colleague has done. He has indicated opposition to the progress of the present act for the reasons he points out and has suggested in his view that the house consider a resolution-
-declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principle, policy, or provisions of the bill-

I do not see that there is in the amendment a declaration of a principle adverse to the principle of the bill before the house. The amendment adds to the provisions of the amending bill but I do not think it sets forth a new principle.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
May I point out that the wording of citation 657 is:
-a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from . . .

I would point out that the resolution which we have put before the house in the terms of this amendment certainly differs from the principles, policy and provisions of the bill in that it asks for a 2 per cent interest rate on money for building homes; and also it differs because it asks for the subsidizing of public housing authorities and that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation go directly into the field of building homes.

May I interrupt the hon. member again, and I hope he does not mind my interrupting him. It seems to me that the first clause of the amendment which proposes that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation issue loans directly to builders at an interest rate of 2 per cent does not differ from any principle in the bill-nor is it adverse to any principle in the bill. speechtext: Yes.
It may foe a different matter but it does not differ from the principle of the bill before the house; it is not adverse to that principle.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Is there not a considerable difference in principle between underwriting the loans by insurance companies at a rate something over 5 per cent and the lending of money directly to builders by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at a rate of 2 per cent? It is because my colleague feels that this proposition should be laid before the house that he believes he comes within the framework of the latter part of the citation which says that he has the right to move a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to the bill. In other words he has the right to ask the house to express itself with regard to the different viewpoint with respect to housing set out in this amendment.
I could recall to Your Honour many occasions on which amendments under citation 657 have been before the house. They cover quite a wide variety of subjects. There have been amendments with respect to a different way of handling redistribution. There have been amendments with respect to a different way of handling the auditing of the Canadian National Railways. There have been amendments with regard to pipe lines, as to whether they should go outside of Canada or stay inside Canada. There have been amendments dealing with the initial price of wheat. There have been amendments dealing *with a different way of handling prairie farm assistance. All of those involved some difference from the proposal in the bill before the house at the time or naturally they would not have been made. It seems to me that the

whole spirit of 657 is that it gives the opposition, when it is not satisfied with a government bill, the right-on second reading-to suggest that the second reading be not now entertained but that a resolution presenting some different principle with respect to the same matter might be considered by the house.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I think you have summed up very well what is implied in this amendment. In the first place, part 1 of the amendment says that the National Housing Act should be amended to permit Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to issue loans directly to the builder at an interest rate of 2 per cent. This provision is beyond the scope of the bill before the house at the moment. In the second place, it is a matter of government policy which, if it were to be implemented, would of necessity have to be preceded by a resolution because it involves the expenditure of money. In my opinion, therefore, it is clearly out of order.

Section 2 of the amendment calls for authority to permit Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to subsidize public housing authorities in order that rents may be brought into line with the financial means of low income dwellers. Section 35 of the National Housing Act already makes adequate provision for subsidization to apply to low rental housing. Section 3 of the amendment is designed to permit Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to enter the field of housing construction to build low rental housing projects where such projects are needed but are not being constructed. There is adequate provision in section 34 of the National Housing Act which has, in fact, already been used for the building of war workers' houses, and more recently rental accommodation for veterans. There is, therefore, adequate provision in the existing legislation to cover sections 2 and 3 of the amendment. I submit, Mr. Speaker, the amendment is therefore out of order.

It seems to be agreed by all members, I think, that sections 2 and 3 of the proposed amendment would be out of order. In any event, I would rule that those two sections are out of order. This, of course, would make the amendment itself out of order because it cannot be partly in order and partly out of order. However, that would leave section 1 of the amendment, and a new amendment with section 1 in it might be submitted. I would be forced to rule that out of order, and I would refer hon. members to
National Housing Act
May's fifteenth edition at page 508 where it is stated:
The principle of relevancy In an amendment governs every such motion.
(1) The amendment must "strictly relate to the bill which the house, by its order, has resolved upon considering" . . .
It seems to me that section 1 of the amendment before the house relates, not to the amending bill which is before the house but to the National Housing Act, 1944. I must rule the amendment out of order.

I believe, Mr. Speaker, that of all the situations which this government has mishandled, it has mishandled the housing situation to a far greater extent than any other. The government has simply refused to face up to the fact that today we have a shortage of half a million houses, and that last year alone that shortage was increased by a further 33,500 much-needed and unbuilt houses. I believe that to try to cure this situation by means of the present legislation is about as effective as trying to cure pneumonia by taking an aspirin tablet.
Because of this government's obsolete and reactionary housing policy, last year we built 20 per cent fewer houses than we built two years ago. Last year, by the government's own admission, there was absolutely no shortage of construction labour or material. The building industry is capable of building
125,000	houses a year, as has been stated on numerous occasions by leaders in the industry. Why then are we building, as we did last year, 70 per cent fewer houses than the construction industry is capable of building, especially in view of the fact that we have an accumulating shortage which today amounts to half a million houses?
I believe there are three reasons for this very disturbing state of affairs. First of all, there is the matter of serviced land. Second, there is the high down payment of 20 per cent demanded on National Housing Act housing, which makes it impossible for a man with an income of less than $5,000 a year to buy a house. Third, the high interest rate and short amortization period under the National Housing Act makes it impossible for a man with a moderate income to carry the charges on a new house.
First of all, I should like to deal with the question of serviced land. Today most municipalities have not got the revenue to pays for schools, roads, water mains, sewers and other local improvements which are necessary to service a housing development. It is obvious, I think, that a builder cannot build houses unless the municipality will allow him to build those houses within the municipal area. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that

National Housing Act
the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) made a very sensible suggestion to overcome this difficulty when he was speaking in this house on November 24 last, as reported at page 33 of Hansard for that date. On that occasion he strongly urged the government, and I quote his words:
To reach agreement with the provincial governments in regard to a clearly defined reallocation of taxing powers so that the provincial governments and municipal councils may have adequate financial resources, to carry out their rapidly increasing responsibilities.
That is the end of his suggestion. I believe if that suggestion is followed by this government, it will overcome the difficulty which municipalities are having today in financing the building of local improvements needed to service new housing developments.
