Now I should like to deal very briefly with the second obstacle to the building of houses, and that is the high down payment demanded by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The cheapest house that you can buy today through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation costs $10,000. You are required to make a 20 per cent down payment which, of course, amounts to $2,000. That virtually excludes any man earning less than $5,000 a year, because in order to put aside that $2,000, you must set aside a minimum of 10 per cent of the $5,000 a year income for a minimum of four years. All of us who have tried to save at one time or another know that it is extremely difficult to set aside 10 per cent of your income for four years in a row. Hence, people earning under $5,000 a year have, for all practical purposes, been excluded from the housing market.
I think it is interesting to examine what has been done in the United States to meet this situation. Under their national housing authority, their down payments are set on a sliding scale. If you buy a house for $7,000, you make a 5 per cent down payment which amounts to $350. When the value of the house increases to $10,000, the down payment is increased to 12 J per cent which amounts to $1,250. I believe that a flat down payment of 10 per cent on a house of $10,000 value or less would serve the purpose more adequately. I believe that this provision would make it possible for people earning a modest income to buy the houses which they so desperately need. The government is following this policy with regard to workers living in defence areas, and I see no reason at all why it should not follow the same policy with respect to workers in non-defence industries.
In the third place, I should like to deal with the question of the interest rate and
TMr. Hees.]
the amortization period. On National Housing Act loans it is necessary to pay 5i per cent interest, and to pay the loan off over a twenty-year period. This requirement makes it extremely difficult indeed for a person earning a modest income to carry the charges on a new house. I should like once again to cite what has been done to meet this situation in the United States. There, loans are made at rates as low as 4 per cent, and the amortization extends over a period as long as thirty years. This provision has made it possible for people earning a modest income to carry the charges on a new house.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that consideration should be given to these policies which have worked out so successfully in the United States, where a greater volume of housing per thousand of population is being built than here in Canada, despite the fact that they are much involved in heavy defence expenditures.
I believe that we should give careful consideration to the policies which have been tried and which have worked out so successfully in the United States. If the kind of policies which I have mentioned were put into force by this government, I believe the building industry would be enabled to build
125,000	houses a year and that those who desperately need houses would find it possible to enter the housing market, and to buy the houses which they so desperately need.

Mr. Speaker, I think this bill is an admission on the part of the government that the present housing act is unsatisfactory, that the money is not available, and that the terms with respect to interest and down payment have been such that people have not been able to build houses as required in this country.
I do not intend to speak at length-and I notice that statement seems to satisfy and to please the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank)-because the hon member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) presented the views of this group in what I thought was an excellently documented speech. I was extremely sorry that his excellent speech did not receive the press coverage it deserved. We find sometimes that someone who comes into the house, makes a few dramatic statements and then walks out again, gets press coverage from one end of Canada to the other. But here the hon. member for York South who speaks with knowledge-who has paid a great deal of attention to the subject in his own constituency, who has studied

it carefully and who knows the situation in his own constituency-and who makes an excellent speech is reported in only a few lines by the press. I think that the press could give more consideration to some of the worth-while speeches we hear in this house rather than, shall I say, to the highlights, the accidental, the incidental and the unusual.
Without a doubt, Mr. Speaker, the speeches that have been made in this house by members on the government side and by many members in the opposition on the question of housing indicate that it is the number one problem facing the Canadian people at the present time. It is one that is close to the Canadian people and they are conscious of it. They are conscious of the need in this respect. I am sure that all hon. members, like myself, have been kept well informed of the shortage of housing in their constituencies, and particularly in the urban sections. I am sure that they also recognize the problem because of an increasing interest on the part of an increasing number of organizations in the housing deficiency at the present time. In my own constituency, Mr. Speaker, I find that the municipalities are becoming concerned. They have had meetings to deal with this question. The Canadian Legion has been concerned about the matter for some years. The trade unions are concerned as also are the women's organizations. Why are they concerned? They become concerned over a situation only when, over a long period of time, there is a definite problem that has not been solved or a definite need that has not been met. It strikes me that at this date, some seven years after the conclusion of the second world war, having regard to our resources and our capacity to produce, we have made little headway in this basically fundamental problem in this country. I know of numbers of young married couples-people who were married two and three years ago -who are still making plans with a view to building a home and have not been able to do so because of the present terms of the National Housing Act, the cost of money, the cost of materials and so on.
Then there is the question of industrial workers who want subsidized low-rental housing, particularly those in the construction industry who move from one point to another. In my constituency there are numbers of these people living in temporary accommodation that could not be considered housing at all. Then we also find that situation with regard to our old age pensioners, our aged people. I will guarantee that in most constituencies in Canada there are still a large number of old age pensioners
National Housing Act
who have not satisfactory accommodation. I know that in my own constituency the problem is so acute that it is being considered by various groups.
Then, as I said the other day, when it comes to the question of immigration, there are two aspects to it. There is the question of placing a man in a job and, second, there is the question of providing him with an opportunity to have a rented home or to build a home under reasonable terms. On that account, Mr. Speaker, this is an increasing and developing problem. Not only do we find it from letters we receive from our constituents, from our personal contacts, and from resolutions by organizations, but the press realize it. This is one problem that I will give the press credit for reporting fairly thoroughly across this country. When meetings are called in connection with housing by various organizations and in various districts, I notice that there is fairly good coverage of the meetings concerned. I think that is because the newspapers realize that this is news to the Canadian people.
I have here a number of clippings taken in recent months from newspapers. Here is one from the Nelson Daily News of January 20, 1953. It is headed:
Housing Canada's Top Social Poser
75,000 homes built in 1952; down payments, interest rates deciding factors in possibility of building.
Then it goes on to explain the difficulties that people are facing in providing themselves with housing. Then I have another one here taken from the Nelson Daily News of October 6, reporting a meeting of the zone conference of the Canadian Legion. The major part of their discussion was over the difficulty encountered by veterans either in building homes or in obtaining satisfactory rental houses. Their conclusions were right along the lines of the amendment moved by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), that the only solution to the question was low cost government housing loans.
Then again, Mr. Speaker, we have the Kootenay Free Press in the city of Trail with an editorial on this question, because it is an acute question there. The conclusion of the editorial is as follows:
A poorly housed, or debt-ridden people, cannot hope to be as productive as those in other lands whose social organization provides a better deal. A recent McLeans survey showed that Canada is behind Britain, Sweden, Australia and the U.S. in provision of adequate housing for people who need it and are willing to pay a reasonable price for it.
Then in the Ottawa Journal of February 24, 1953, there appears an article under the headline: "Aid to the Small Home Buyer urged in Ontario Legislature."

National Housing Act
That is the story from the Atlantic to the Pacific, in all our urban communities. People living in a land of wealth are seeking houses and are unable to obtain them. What is most important is this. Since the conclusion of the war we have had a tremendous industrial expansion in this country, and we welcome it. In my own constituency immense sums of money have been spent in the building of dams. The sum of $33 million was spent in the building of one dam, $20 million for another smelter, and millions in the development of the saw mill industry. It is proposed to invest $75 million in a pulp mill. That picture is reflected all across the country. While we can build these huge industrial enterprises, we do not seem to be able to build houses for the people to live in who are going to produce and use these industrial tools that have been manufactured in such quantities. I am not blaming any individual. It is not a question of individuals. I know the minister does all he can under the terms of the legislation. I know he is most concerned and most active in regard to this question. It is therefore not a question of individuals; but our whole economy is based on the principle of profits first. Because there is not the same profit in house building we consider profits first and people's welfare second. That is not our intention, but that is the way the system works. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, we have to do something in this parliament to remedy that situation, and I am sure we can do something if we have the will and the understanding of the situation.
This group has been particularly concerned over this question for many years. In fact, this was the only group in the house during the depression period that suggested that the unemployed could very well be kept employed by building houses across the country. If the advice of the C.C.F. group in the house during the depression had been taken we would not have the shortage of houses that exists at the present time.
We are interested in this because we believe in the sacredness of human personality, and you cannot develop human personality to its ultimate unless you have people living in good houses and give them the opportunity to develop a sound and proper home life.
There is no question about the orthodox methods having failed to build the required number of houses or to provide the required number of houses in Canada at this time. We have been nibbling at this question since 1945 and we have not advanced very far along the road. We have not been able today to take up the lag, and the new family ranks are greater each year than the new houses that are being built. That is why we in

this group proposed the amendment that you recently ruled out of order, Mr. Speaker. We believe that if this problem is to be met we must use the national credit; we must take what I presume are, from the point of view of the government and possibly from the point of view of the Conservative party, unusual measures. But we have the Bank of Canada; we have the collective credit of the people of Canada. We believe that that institution should be used so that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation could issue loans directly to builders at an interest rate of 2 per cent. We think that is urgently necessary if we are to build the houses that the people need.
I was interested in reading a memorandum presented to the dominion government by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada on Thursday, March 24, 1949. There is a paragraph in this brief on housing which I shall read:
The shortage of homes in most sections of the country is still critical. Many resolutions and reports dealing with the housing shortage came before our recent convention. The consensus of opinion was that the housing crisis continues to become more acute.
That is quite correct. I continue:
The guaranteeing of credits offers little remedy and the position previously taken by this congress was reaffirmed.
We therefore request the dominion government to undertake, in co-operation with provincial and municipal governments, a nation-wide low rental home building program financed by national credit and designed to house, under decent conditions, ex-service personnel and those in low income brackets who cannot afford the high building costs of today.
We agree absolutely with that resolution. The situation is more serious today than it was when this brief was brought before the dominion government in 1945 by the representatives of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada. It is a sound proposition. I am not one to suggest the use of credit on an unsound basis. This is a capital investment which is self-liquidating and which will return not only the capital and the 2 per cent interest but huge dividends in human happiness and in increased productivity at this time. That is why we suggest the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should subsidize public housing in order that rents may be brought in line with the financial means and the income of low income dwellers.
The hon. member for York South dealt with this matter, as did the previous speaker. I refer to the municipalities and the importance of enabling them to carry the cost of refinancing loans and so on that are required for the extension of housing in the various communities. In addition to that we urge that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation

enter the field of housing construction and build low-rental housing projects where such projects are now not being constructed. We believe that some policy along the lines that we have suggested is the only policy that will meet the situation. The need is so great that even this government, with all its reluctance to use the national credit in the way we suggest, should take that step and take it immediately.
To see the value of subsidized housing, just look at the success we have had with the building of houses under the small holdings provision of the Veterans Land Act. The Department of Veterans Affairs has done an excellent job in that respect. There are some improvements that we should like to see in the regulations and in the act, but on the whole they have done an excellent job. Why? Because the government in that legislation recognized that the pressing need of a veteran on returning home was a house. They have subsidized the building of the houses to the extent of something over $2,100 on a $6,000 house. That has proved very successful. In my own constituency I know of dozens and dozens of veterans, who are now industrial workers, who have taken advantage of the terms of the small holding section of the Veterans Land Act and have had the opportunity to enjoy the subsidy. As a result of that you will see dozens and dozens of neat cottages placed on a half acre of ground with lawns and gardens around them. What have you got? You have contented workers and happy families and improved working conditions, and these workers are taking a most active and increasing interest in the communities in which they live. You have happiness; you have progress and you have production as a result of that investment of government funds in the subsidies given to these men. That is a good illustration of what could be done by the subsidization of the building of houses generally in Canada at this time.
The principle has been proven sound. If we can subsidize gold mines to carry on, if we can subsidize other industries in this country, surely we should subsidize the building of houses. For what does industry mean in Canada today, what does wealth mean, what do profits mean unless the people are able to live in houses, to erect houses and build a satisfactory home life?
I do urge the minister to give some consideration to the representations of this group. We do not make them on a partisan basis; we make them in all sincerity because we are in very close touch with the need. I know the minister has a warm and generous heart, and I would hope that before the bill 68108-283
National Housing Act
is given second reading, and goes through committee stage, he would introduce some amendments which would indicate that he has listened favourably to the pleas of members of this group, and other members in the house.
I had not intended to speak at length, but I shall deal briefly with one or two matters of particular interest to my own constituency. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has built a very excellent group of houses at Sunningdale, a suburb of Trail. There are veteran tenants in these houses. It is a delightful community, one of the most pleasing in that area. The occupants have taken great care of their houses by improving the interiors and the exteriors, as well as the grounds.
Quite recently 175 of these veterans sent a petition and brief to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation urging that they be given the opportunity to buy these houses. The brief received the support of the corporation of Trail, and I would ask the minister and his officials to give serious consideration to their requests. These men are workers for the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. The occupants of these homes are proud of them and they want to have ownership. They have been tenants for a number of years and would now like to change their status. I do hope the minister and the officials in his department will receive these representations favourably. It would mean an increase in revenue for Trail and help the city out considerably. Title to these houses would be another incentive to the men to develop the properties.
One other matter has been brought to my attention, and that is the classification of defence workers. Those who have been employed in the plant of Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company have been classified as defence workers, because it is a defence plant. That has been of some advantage to the workers. However, I have here correspondence with a group of which has not been able to take advantage of this classification. The plant of Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company is within the municipality of Tadanac. The fire brigade of that municipality is occupied principally with the prevention of fires in the plant of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. I would suppose that 99-999 per cent of their duties would be those of protecting the plant of the company from the ravages of fire.
These men have written to me and to other groups suggesting that those who are connected with the fire brigade are taking an essential part in defence production and should be classified as defence workers. My understanding is that at the present time the act and regulations do not permit this. I

National Housing Act
would ask the minister to give consideration to an amendment which would make provision tor these men who are giving an essential service to a defence industry, so that they might be classified as defence workers, and be placed in the same position as the actual workers in the plant.
Hon. members in this group do not intend to take a great deal of time in this debate, but we are greatly concerned with this problem. We do urge the minister and his officials to give consideration to our representations; because we know that houses mean happiness and health, and health and happiness mean production, and the whole means stability. And all these will be needed to build our future progress.

Mr. Speaker, it was interesting to hear the speeches today about the subject of housing, some of which were thought-provoking, and others simply provoking. It can never be assessed properly unless one is willing to do it in a dispassionate fashion.
Housing is a subject which has aroused considerable emotion in the breasts of some previous speakers. Obviously it is also a very important subject. Unless hon. members are willing to get at the facts and unless they are willing to be dispassionate about it, they cannot solve the problem or find a solution for it.
I have heard today various figures about the backlog and the shortage of housing. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) has said the backlog amounted to
700,000	houses. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) has said it is 500,000 houses; and various other figures have been given. It is very easy, through the bureau of vital statistics, to determine how many families are in Canada at a given time and how many houses there are, and it is easy to see the discrepancy between the two figures.
But the backlog is an entirely different problem. A great many of those who have not houses are not in a position to buy houses, and will never be in a position to buy houses, and some do not even want to buy them. And these figures indicating the backlog or the shortage of housing are not conclusive. I have never seen a figure yet as to the backlog of housing which has been on an actuarially sound basis, or a basis which could be mathematically determined. They take all kinds of bases for these figures, and they certainly are not sound.
But let us assume that there is some backlog and some shortage of houses. Not long ago I wrote a letter to the dominion bureau of statistics asking for some information about the greater Toronto area. I asked them how 
many families were there in 1951, and how many housing units in that year. At that time in the greater metropolitan area of Toronto they showed that there were 302,381 families in the census. They also showed that at that time there were 273,200 housing units in the area, which indicates a discrepancy between the two figures of about
27.000.	And when one considers how many of those 27,000 are perhaps newly married people, or people with small incomes and would not be in a position to buy houses, and how many may never want to buy houses, and when you consider the percentage who are not in a position to take houses, and who perhaps do not want them, the discrepancy is impossible to estimate. But obviously it is not as great as this figure of
27.000.
Let us assume it is only half that figure, which leaves us with, roughly, 13,500 families requiring housing. That is not a very large percentage of units out of the
300.000.	So that the discrepancy or the backlog is not as great as has been indicated. I am not saying there is no shortage, but certainly it is not as great as has been indicated by previous speakers.
The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), in his usual scolding manner, was rather abusive of the efforts of the government. But, frankly, I expect that from him, because I never have heard him any other way-never. However, I do agree with his concluding remarks in which he congratulated the minister upon his ability and upon the satisfactory administration of his department.
Then the hon. member says that for the six post-war years we have had 495,000 houses and that we have 513,000 family formations. I would point out that that figure of family formations is difficult to determine. It is easy to determine the number of families who come in through immigration. That can be done through the immigration office, because that is where they have to go. But when they come separately it is hard to tie it up-that is, when husbands, wives and children come at different times.
Then, it is easy to tell by the number of marriages how many new families we have, but it is difficult to determine how many old families, through deaths, are broken up. So I say that the figure of net family formations is a nebulous one, and that it is most inconclusive. I believe anyone who has studied the problem will recognize that it is a very unsound figure, or that at best it is a "guesstimate". So that when the hon. member says that there is a discrepancy between houses and family formations of just over
17.000.	I suggest to him that that may not be

so at all. It may not be half of that, it may not be quarter of that. It is just a figure you cannot arrive at or determine accurately.
It may be double that.

National Housing Act
builder comes to them with a plan for a hundred acres, or whatever it is, they say they will approve it if he will put in the roads, guarantee the school debentures, put in the storm sewers, the water mains, the gutters and so on. All these items of service drive up the cost of the houses because they all cost money.
This serviced land problem is not an easy one to solve. It can be determined only over a period of years. Possibly because of the thoughtlessness or possibly the ignorance of municipal councils in the past, builders were permitted to put up houses wherever they wanted to. They did not recognize the difficulty they were getting into. They did not appreciate the type of schools that were going to be built.
The schools being built today are of a much more expensive architecture. The one-floor, ranch-type school is beautiful, but it is too expensive. This problem is not going to be solved for a number of years. But it will be solved because gradually the urban municipalities will get the required 35 per cent or more of industry and gradually they will have more land available for housing. It is not a problem that can be solved quickly. People who say that you can solve this housing problem overnight are just not facing the facts of our constitutional and financial set-up. They suggest that we should change all these things, but that would make only for greater confusion.
Another suggestion was that the down payment should be much less, possibly no more than 10 per cent. But does that solve the problem? With a down payment of 10 per cent you immediately require a loan of $9,000 instead of $8,000, and that increases the monthly amortization payments. Under the regulations of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation the monthly payment, including interest, principal and taxes, should not be more than 23 per cent of the person's salary. You would be surprised at how many people would be brought outside that provision of 23 per cent if an extra $1,000 were added to their loans. Most purchasers of these low-cost $10,000 homes are buying them within a very few dollars of the 23 per cent provision. As soon as you add another $1,000 to the loan you defeat your purpose-you would then have houses but you would have no purchasers.
The hon. member, along with others, suggests that the interest rate is too high and the amortization period too short. As I have said already, if we are going to get the lending institutions to put their money into the mortgage field the mortgage interest rate must be at a level which will attract them away
(Mr. Hunter.]
from other investments. It is all very well for the members of the socialist party down there to say that we do not need these financial institutions, that we can get the money through taxes so that the government can put out its own funds. But I do not want to pay any more taxes and I do not think most people in Canada want to pay any more taxes. I think they are quite content to leave the lending institutions in the field. They realize that the lending institutions, being trustees for the policyholders' money, cannot lend out their money at any unduly low rate of interest.
I must say in fairness to the lending institutions that most of them have been very appreciative of this critical period in housing. I think you will find that most of the lending institutions of this country are putting out a much greater percentage of the current money they have available, in the form of mortgage loans, than they would normally have done. These companies have very attractive investments open in other fields; yet most of them, with some humanitarian feeling, have put out a very much greater percentage of money available, for mortgage loans, than they would otherwise have done. I know that is true and I think that most members of the house know that it is true. They have been very co-operative but, naturally, they cannot go to the point of losing money which belongs to their policyholders.
As a holder of insurance in this house- and I presume everyone else here holds insurance-I do not think we want the lending institutions to endanger the money that is being invested on their behalf.
The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) suggested that the housing problem was very great and very critical. Well, if he had said that five years ago he would have been right. I do not say that there is no problem but it cannot be considered to be as great a problem or as critical a problem as it was five years ago. There is getting to be a very close approach to the necessary housing. You only have to look at the figures in a city like my own-Toronto-which is considered to have a very critical shortage of housing. It is one of the few hot spots for lack of housing in Canada. You will find that where houses were once sold before completion, now the period between completion and sale is steadily lengthening, even for cheaper housing. That, I think, indicates that the shortage is being met. It is completely unrealistic for people like the hon. member for York South to get up and say that costs have passed beyond the reach of tens of thousands of people in Canada, as if it were something that had just walked in, something

that had happened under this government. Where in any country in the world has everybody always had a house? There is no country in the world that has a housing supply as close to family formations as Canada has-with perhaps the exception of the United States. I have seen figures in magazines which say that the construction of housing in Canada is falling behind compared with the United States, England, Australia and so on. Well, in Australia they do not even put in any heating. They build prefabricated boxes and call their effort a housing program. In England what are they building? Not what we would call houses- and to compare the two situations is not fair at all. In fact, the record of this parliament, this government and this- administration with respect to housing is second to none in the world.
I hear laughter and I think it probably comes from the socialists, who feel that everybody must have a house. Well, I think that is a beautiful ideal; I think it is a lofty ideal and I think we should strive for it; but I do not think we are going to have that millennium tomorrow. I think the theories of the socialists are delightful because they remind me of the fairy stories I used to read as a little lad. They make delightful reading but they are completely crazy.
Now let us get to the matter of availability of mortgage money. Where is this mortgage money coming from, and how much do we need? I think that last year there was something around $700 million-and how much mortgage money do we need to completely meet the housing shortage that everyone feels is so clearly indicated in Canada? Well, I do not think that anyone knows. I do not see how anyone can know because no one knows what the shortage is. All we know is that we can only govern the number of houses built by the demand. How else can we know? It is all very well to pull these figures out of the sky and say that there is a backlog of 500,000, which was the figure given by one hon. member, and to say that there is a backlog of 700,000-the figure given by another hon. member. There is just a small discrepancy of 200,000 units. That shows you how completely nebulous and inaccurate the figures are. There is only one way to determine the shortage of housing and that is from the demand for them. It is the same as it is for shirts. If there is a shortage of shirts they sell rapidly but if there are plenty of shirts they stay on the shelves. The same situation applies to everything in a free enterprise country, and as soon as you get away from a free enterprise system you might as well fold up, because you have entered
National Housing Act
into the deadest thing that has ever happened-socialism.
I have gone into these things because I do not think they have had fair treatment. I do not think that people have been facing the facts in the world-that we have a free enterprise system. I do not think they have been facing the importance, or the value and the strength of our free enterprise system. It is a system which is stronger than anything else and so much better that these other things are just not comparable. No one thinks that the free enterprise system is perfect. Why should it be perfect? How can it be perfect-when human beings are running it? It is just silly to think it should be. That is why socialism is so stupid, because it assumes that human beings are perfect. The socialists take the latter as being a very lofty assumption and I can only hope that they are examples of what we are going to have in that perfect society. I think that occasionally even they have their human weaknesses, and those human weaknesses will tear down anything.
One socialist says that we must get rid of that profit motive. That is just about the silliest thing I have heard. What other motive is there? What is going to motivate people to get out and do something? There is just the profit motive. I do wish that every person in this country were Christian enough not to require the profit motive to do things for their fellow men, but I do not think that even the hon. member who made the statement would really agree that such is the case. There are quite a few people who are not entirely motivated by Christian love. It is foolish and it is the fallacy of the whole socialist system-and it always will be. I do not think that in our time human beings are going to be perfect.
I would like to congratulate the minister on the job that he has done. He has dealt with these matters with tolerance, understanding, energy, and a great deal of determination. I do not always agree with him and I think that we have had a few words from time to time. I have sometimes felt afterwards that I was right, but even though I may not always agree with him I think that on the whole his attitude toward the question of housing has been one of deep interest, deep penetration, and I think that this government has been very lucky to have him handling this subject.
I would also like to say a word for the officials who are running Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. While I have had differences with them I have found them a singularly intelligent bunch. I have found them hard-working, very interested in their subject and co-operative within their terms

National Housing Act
of reference. I have formed a very high regard for the administration of the corporation. Although it is perhaps not nice to mention names, I would also like to say a few words about Angus McClaskey whose head office for Ontario is in Toronto. He is a very hard-headed Scot, a man completely interested in housing and for whom I have the highest regard. He is a man who I think has done a splendid job.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to speak again on this subject because it was only last Tuesday, April 21, that I did speak at quite some length upon it. At that time I put forward a proposal which I thought would be of assistance to the government and the people of Canada, and of particular assistance to those people who are in dire need of housing. I was amazed, however, at the remarks of the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Hunter), who has just taken his seat. I cannot recall exactly what he said when he referred to the number of houses in Canada but I think he said that the need expressed by some hon. members was greatly exaggerated. In fact, he added that there were very few people in Canada who needed a house. He said it might be a matter of a few thousand.

Mr. Speaker, I want to object ;o that kind of interpretation being put upon my words. I was speaking strictly of Toronto where I said there was a shortage of 27,000. I do not want to be misinterpreted.
I was not misinterpreting you. If I heard you correctly you have just now said 20,000-
Twenty-seven thousand.

I will not argue over whether it is 20,000 or 27,000 but I cannot help but recall the remarks which the hon. member has just made about standing behind the minister, that the minister has done a wonderful job, and that anything the minister has said has been perfectly correct. I am not disputing that but I want to make perfectly clear just what the minister did say about the shortage of housing. I mentioned it in Hansard for Tuesday, April 21. The Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) was speaking to the Appraisal Institute of Canada, I think it was, on Thursday April 2, 1953, when he had something to say about the shortage of housing. I am sure the member for Parkdale (Mr. Hunter) would not contradict the Minister of Resources and Development. Now, you just listen to what he said there, and then compare that with
rMr. Hunter.]
your statement. He is speaking of low rental housing, and this is what the article said:
Mr. Winters said that not more than one-third of Canada's families could afford new houses- either to rent or to own.
Do you mean to tell me that there are only
27,000	people in Canada who need houses, when the minister himself says that at least one-third

The hon. member obviously does not understand what I said. I spoke of the Toronto and York area, and said there was a discrepancy of 27,000 between the actual family units and the housing accommodation. At no time did I say that was all in Canada or anywhere else.

It is very fine now for the
hon. member for Parkdale to get up and make a correction in what he said. If this same relationship which applies to Toronto were to be applied to the rest of Canada, then the hon. member's estimate of the Toronto area is away out, too. Then, this article goes on to say:
But if enough new houses weren't found, he stated, it would affect the people at the bottom of the scale-the people who were living in dilapidated and obsolescent houses.
Anyone who gets up and tells us there is no great need for housing in Canada, when the minister himself has been honest in showing the great need for it, obviously does not know what the situation is. I think it would have been much more appropriate if the hon. member for Parkdale had been speaking of trying to maintain the loan companies and insurance companies in this country rather than maintaining housing. The whole of his argument was that we could not expect them to lend money at 2 per cent to build houses, but rather that they should lend it at 5J per cent, not for the purpose of building houses but in order to keep the financial institutions and mortgage people in a sound financial position. I may tell him that the whole housing program was started, not to build houses but to keep the mortgage and loan companies in a solvent position.
We started out by granting moneys through the loan companies at 4 per cent. As soon as the field got to a point where these companies could lend money on other enterprises at greater amounts of interest they did not lend money to build houses. They came to the government and said: Unless you give us a greater increase in our interest rates we cannot afford to lend money to build houses; we will lend it out in places where we can get a greater return. From a business point of view I am not arguing against that. I am saying that is not the way to build houses.

Our experience has shown that when the loan companies take that attitude, then we do not get houses built. My concern, Mr. Speaker, is to see that we build some houses for these people to whom the minister was referring, the two-thirds of the families in Canada who cannot afford to own or rent houses.
Now, the members of the C.C.F. party proposed an amendment a while ago which was ruled out of order. I want to say that so far as the proposition was concerned I did not think it was so very far out of line. I thought some of the clauses needed polishing a bit and brought more into line with good business practice, but in general I thought the proposition was fairly good. I would not want the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) to get away with the statement he made a while ago. He said that during the depression the C.C.F. party was the only party which advocated the issuance of national credit. He was so wrong in that statement that he did not know what he was talking about. If he will go back and examine the record, he will find that what I am saying is true. The Social Credit party has always advocated the issuance of national credit. I could say some more about that, but I just wanted to draw that to his attention.
What I want to say today, Mr. Speaker, is related to what the minister referred to in his speech on April 21. I do not intend to repeat what I said the other day concerning the National Housing Act. As I indicated a while ago, I spoke then at some length. The minister was speaking about the necessity for housing, but in his speech this afternoon he did not indicate any way in which we were going to change this present plan of house building in order to meet the situation of those people who, under the present set-up, cannot afford to build these homes. When I was speaking the other day I offered a proposal. I do not know whether or not the government will take it. I would have introduced it in the form of an amendment, except that I am sure the Speaker would have found some ruling whereby it could have been declared out of order. I did not, therefore, submit it as an amendment.
I am quite sure that the plan which I proposed would assist us in the building of houses. The minister had something to say about that, and I want to refer to it because he made mention of the province of Alberta. I had said that the province set up a revolving fund to take care of serviced land for self-liquidating projects. I was fully aware of the fact that that project was not for the purpose of assisting under section 35 of the National Housing Act. What I was pointing
National Housing Act
out to the minister was that if they did set up a plan for a revolving fund, then the provinces would be able to co-operate under that plan and extend their present system for self-liquidating projects to be included under section 35. At page 4169 of Hansard lor April 21, 1953, the minister said:
Now, the Alberta government has a revolving fund. One of the techniques the federal government has at its disposal is co-operation with the provincial governments, and we do that under section 35. As I understand it the Alberta legislation was amended this year to discontinue having money from that revolving fund flow into municipal works through section 35. If a municipality wishes to benefit by the co-operative plan under section 35 it must now go into the open market to get its money. The Alberta revolving fund is no longer available. I do not wish to be critical of the government on that point. They probably did that because they felt it was in the best interests of the people they served. I merely cite that as a matter of fact.
I want to speak about that for a moment. Under the proposal which I offered the other day I suggested that, if the government would set up this revolving fund, then the provinces, not only Alberta but the other provinces, would be able to put in a plan similar to that which Alberta has for the self-liquidating project, thus enabling them to supply serviced land. There is no sense in the provincial government setting up a revolving fund and lending that money at 2 per cent for the loan companies or mortgage companies to come in and build houses on that serviced land for which they are charging the people 51 per cent. The only thing that would accomplish would be to give greater security to the loan companies. What sense is there in that? That is not going to solve our problem. What you would be doing, in effect, would be subsidizing the loan companies. I would not advocate a thing like that, and I would be surprised if the provinces would tolerate such a condition. If the federal government sets up a revolving fund to build homes at 2 per cent, then I am sure the provinces will co-operate by lending money to the municipalities at 2 per cent for self-liquidating projects in order to provide serviced land. I do not want anybody here to get the impression that the lending companies are going to be so benevolent as the hon. member for Parkdale said, and will break their necks trying to build homes regardless of profit.
The revolving fund is still there.
Yes. As the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) points out, the revolving fund is still available in the province of Alberta for the purpose for which it was set up.

Not under section 35.

National Housing Act

No; and you could not blame them. Why would they lend money out at 2 per cent for servicing land and then have the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the loan companies come in and build their houses on that already serviced land at 2 per cent, and charge 5J per cent to the people who are going to build houses? Then they would have the serviced land already there which increases the value of the property of the mortgage company, with better security than they had before. Rather than spending our money to finance the loan companies at 2 per cent, we might better buy Ontario bonds and get 3 j per cent or 4 per cent, if you are going to be cold-blooded about the thing. I never saw an instance where the mortgage companies went out of their way to assist the home builders, but I can indicate many places where they went out of their way to gyp the home owner; and I could refer to a court record in proving my argument. When anybody stands up here and tells me how benevolent the loan companies have been in even seeing that the loans made to these prospective owners are properly administered, he has to prove it to me because my experience does not bear that out.
There may be some grounds for the subsidizing of low-rental projects. The C.C.F. members had that provision in one of the clauses of their amendment, but it was declared to be out of order. There probably is a group which-and I am sure there is- no matter how low the down payment was, still could not afford to buy homes. Under those circumstances it may be necessary to have some type of subsidization by the federal government whereby those houses can be built; then they will have to be rented having in mind the ability of the individual to pay.
When I was down in the United States a year ago-just about a year ago now-I saw some of the projects there in New York; they were beautiful apartment houses and they were rented at low monthly rates. The rents being received were based entirely upon the ability of the individual to pay, and they were about $25, $26 and $27 a month. You could not hope to build such a structure as that and have the cost of building paid back through the rent received. Hence in this case it would be necessary for some type of subsidization to house those people who, no matter how low the down payment was, would never be able to own a house. But if the government would enter into some new plan that would definitely show results in building houses so that people might own them-such as the plan I suggested, or some other similar one-I am quite convinced that we would find the province to be extremely

co-operative; because it is the desire of the provinces as well as that of the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) to see our people properly housed. I am sure that Alberta would be one of the first to co-operate. But I would not expect them to co-operate in servicing land, thereby further enhancing the security of mortgage and the loan companies. In my opinion that is not the purpose of the national housing program. Its purpose should be to build houses at prices at which our people can afford to buy them. You cannot have better security; and you cannot have more contented people than those who live in their own homes. I trust that the minister will give this idea some further consideration.

Mr. Speaker, there are just one or two observations I wish to make in connection with this bill to amend the National Housing Act. They cover my own province of Saskatchewan in general and Saskatoon in particular. I refer to a matter that was drawn to the attention of the minister on March 30 last as reported at page 3403 of Hansard when a question was asked by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) with regard to the situation that prevailed there and the difficulty in the province of Saskatchewan of securing loans from loan companies in order to permit the building of houses by builders.
First, may I say that I was greatly interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Hunter) when he eulogized in such fulsome measure the benefits of free enterprise and received from the members supporting the government that warm applause which is indicative of the fact that, as they applauded, they did not realize that no government in history-even the socialist government of Saskatchewan-has so far embarked on so many measures of a socialistic nature and a denial of free enterprise as has this government. Having said that, I want to refer particularly to the situation in Saskatoon which has already been brought to the attention of the minister. It has to do with the housing situation there, and it also indirectly has to do with the housing situation generally in Saskatchewan. I think I can follow no better course than simply to refer to the resolution which was presented to the city council by the Saskatoon home builders' association some two weeks after the minister on March 30 set out something of the house building that has taken place in Saskatoon, and the increase in building there during the year 1952, as an answer to or a denial of the request that was made on that day by the hon. member for Saskatoon.

This brief sets forth particularly a situation, as I said, that prevails in Saskatoon and one that also requires attention in other cities in the province. It is becoming more difficult in Saskatchewan, as time goes on, to get mortgage loans under the National Housing Act. There are authorized companies that will not lend in Saskatchewan, although they lend in other western provinces. In Saskatoon it has been found that these loan companies have been drastically reducing the amount of money they will lend here. The result is that the financial handicaps that are imposed by the companies, when they do make loans, make it increasingly difficult for deserving people in Saskatoon in particular and in Saskatchewan generally to own their own homes. The portion of the brief that is material reads as follows:
And whereas the majority of the builders operating in other cities in Canada have been granted selling prices which did permit them during 1952 to build and obtain 80 per cent loans, few of the builders in Saskatoon have been granted selling prices under which they can work and permit their purchasers to obtain these larger loans . . . The mortgage companies as well as Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have appeared unwilling to increase their lending values in Saskatoon over the amount set three years ago while in the meantime building costs have greatly increased because of higher wages demanded by labour and increases in freight rates on lumber, cement, plaster, plaster board, brick, flue lining, hardware, furnaces, plumbing fixtures . . .
-and the like. I point out that there is a problem there because many of these requirements, as the minister knows, must necessarily come from a considerable distance. As to building materials in Saskatchewan, there is no shortage in so far as lumber and the like are concerned. Those materials are readily procurable there; but in the main we are faced with the very serious increase in freight rates. Even though those rates are applicable to all parts of Canada, they do particularly affect that province because of the need to import building materials from the other provinces. The brief goes on:
It is further apparent that Saskatchewan builders have not been allowed as part of their cost the 3 per cent education and hospitalization tax which they must pay on the cost of all material being used, which amounts to from $209 to $300 per house.
Consideration should be given in that regard. Certainly there are three provinces -and I am speaking from memory

that have these direct taxes, and some consideration should be given, as requested in this brief, to builders in these provinces. I understand that New Brunswick, Quebec and of course Saskatchewan impose this tax. The brief goes on:
And whereas this shortage of mortgage money has drastically reduced the number of homes which the builders could have built, and in addition has increased the cost of building because of the
National Housing Act
limited operations. The result is that the builders have been unable to erect sufficient homes to satisfy the popular demand and consequently there has been a continual agitation to have more publicly financed homes built in the city.
And whereas some of the companies which had been loaning here and which until very recently said they had little or no money for Saskatoon this year, have now intimated they will make some money available-
There is an improvement in the situation.
Nevertheless the mortgage money outlook for Saskatoon, for 1953, is greatly restricted compared with past years, is very disappointing, and greatly handicaps the builders in their ability and willingness to provide homes for those who wish to own their own.
And finally the request is that consideration be given to the improvement of the situation there. The brief goes on to say:
While these are the same regulations that apply in other Canadian cities, they create a much more serious problem in Saskatoon than elsewhere because the builders in other cities are being granted enough speculative loans to proceed with normal construction. In Saskatoon where the majority of loans are home-owner applications, these numerous obstructions and handicaps prevent the builders from proceeding with the erection of homes in any large number.
The request that is finally made is that:
If the mortgage companies are unable or unwilling to make it (the National Housing Act) fully operative here, we request that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation apply to Saskatoon their agency agreement which has been extended to communities of less than 50,000 population.
That applies not only to Saskatoon but to a lesser extent to the city of Regina. It is something that is very necessary, and if granted by the minister through amendment of the regulations it would achieve a considerable increase in housing accommodation in Saskatchewan, in the cities of Saskatoon and Regina.
I know that in the operation of the act changes must be made from time to time to meet the exigencies of changing conditions. This act represents an endeavour to meet a situation that challenges the initiative of this or any other government that might be in power, and the act must necessarily be subject to periodical changes in order to meet the changes in circumstances as they arise. While the act as it was and the regulations as they were did meet the situation to a degree, nevertheless the changes asked for in this brief-and I think they are generally supported in Saskatoon and Regina; I have just returned from a couple of days in northern Saskatchewan-if made would go a long way toward rectifying the situation.
Certainly no one wants the government embarking on an expenditure orgy such as was contemplated in such horrendous terms by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Hunter); but on the other hand the govern-

National Housing Act
ment, having embarked on a policy of endeavouring to provide housing accommodation for so large a portion of the population as is possible, should endeavour to remove those anomalies which exist in the law or the regulations, and which in any way tend to reduce that maximum production of building units which is the avowed purpose of the legislation. In other words, as I see the picture what Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is in effect doing is operating a partnership as between socialism on the one hand and free enterprise on the other, with the end in view of securing the greatest good for the greatest number. The minister nods his head in agreement with that general summary.
I know there is pronounced criticism of the failure of the corporation to achieve that degree of perfection which would provide houses for everyone. That is an ideal which will always remain an ideal. But when a situation prevails such as that in Saskatchewan, with the provincial problem incident to the education tax and the fact which cannot be denied that loan companies have greatly restricted the field of their lending operations for housing, there is a need, and a very challenging one, for a change in the regulations in order to meet the request of the builders' association, which is reinforced by a general public demand for a change in the regulations.
I make this in the form of an appeal to the minister, that he give further consideration to the rather abrupt refusal he uttered on March 30 to the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight), and that the situation be canvassed and reconsidered to the end that this legislation shall be made effective everywhere in Canada; so that one or two provinces will not enjoy the benefits of the legislation to an extent beyond that which, in proportion to the population, all provinces should enjoy.
On that basis I feel that Saskatchewan has legitimate grounds for complaint. While the minister may be able to point out that there has been an increase in units, that increase is infinitesimal as compared with the demand for increased housing this year, which will not be met in the cities of Saskatchewan that I mentioned unless these and possibly other changes are made, and which from experience the minister will know have to be made to meet a situation that requires immediate attention.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to take very long in this debate, because I have already spoken about housing in the debate which took place in

February. It was a year ago that I brought to the attention of the house the fact that the lending institutions were withdrawing to more profitable fields, and vacating the field that was historically theirs. I am glad to see that now I have allies in other parts of the house who have come to the same conclusion; perhaps if we join together we shall be effective.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Come on over.

There is more room over on my side. The minister told us today that the most pressing problem in the production of housing was the need for serviced land. I think it is the conclusion of hon. members, from what has already been said, that the most pressing problem is the shortage of mortgage money. The minister indicated that life and fire insurance, trust and loan companies were the main sources of private mortgage money. He told us today that their mortgage holdings represent a quarter of their total assets. I have no doubt his figures are correct; but it is not enough.
Mr. Fortin, secretary-treasurer of the dominion mortgage and investment association, said, in response to a request for mortgage money, "But there is not enough money to go around". He said that some projects must be postponed, and that house-building mortgages must take their share of the postponement. His words appear in the Globe and Mail of March 25, 1953.
Last year Mr. Mansur, giving evidence before the standing committee on banking and commerce, said that 10,000 additional starts would have been made if mortgage money had been available in 1952. This means that we lost the use of some 10,000 houses during 1952 because we did not have enough mortgage money. That is a very serious matter.
Since 1947, under section 31A of the National Housing Act, there is authority to the corporation to make loans on its own account when joint loans are not available from lending institutions. To meet the shortage of mortgage money, direct loans have been made available in municipalities under 5,000. In August of 1952 that was extended to communities under 50,000, such as Oshawa, Barrie, Brampton, Orillia and similar municipalities. Then today the minister said in his statement:
The introduction of the agency arrangement in 1952 by which the corporation extended the direct loan facilities of section 31A to cities of from 5,000 to 50,000 population is already a step in that direction.
Up to the present time 96 loans have been made under that section of the act. The minister knows how disappointing that is, in

my view; because we are not coming to grips with the problem. I think that in the main the minister and the government are doing an excellent job on housing; but a new problem has arisen, and we are not facing up to it. Financing today, above all things, is limiting our ability to build houses. There just is not enough money now available to build homes. Therefore credit-worthy Canadians cannot obtain the money which ought to be available to them.
I recall very well when the occasion arose in the house to increase interest rates. It was then said-I do not suggest it was said by the minister but certainly it was said outside the house-that if we wanted to make it attractive to the mortgage companies we had to increase the interest rates. Well, we did that; and almost immediately more money came on the scene. Now we find we are getting another squeeze. I am suggesting to the house that this is another attempt being made to increase interest rates once again.
If there is no inclination on the part of the government to expand the loan program, surely there is an opportunity to increase the joint loan. At the present time we are participants to the extent of 25 per cent. We could participate to the extent of 50 per cent, which would make 25 per cent more money available to the public generally by way of conventional or direct loans from the mortgage companies. This would help the mortgage companies to provide available funds in order to provide more housing.
I think it would do more than that. What I am saying to the house is that if we participated to the extent of 50 per cent instead of 25 per cent it would also decrease the fear of the lending institutions against a lower down payment, or a longer amortization period. Consequently it would make it easier for people in Canada who need houses to obtain them.
If more mortgage money was available at the present time it would have an effect upon construction costs. If builders were able to plan so that they could use mass-production methods and undertake large-scale building projects, they could bring down the cost of housing. But they are unable to do that at the present time, because they cannot obtain forward commitments for mortgages.
I am considerably disappointed to find that it is necessary for us to beg money from lending institutions, on their terms; still it is not available to a great many Canadians who do not want it for speculation purposes, but merely to build homes. In the House of Commons we talk about encouraging people to live in their own homes. That is the way it should be. But on the other hand we are
National Housing Act
not doing too much to make that possible. I think the time has come when a creditworthy Canadian ought to be able to obtain whatever funds he requires to build a home for himself and his family. If mortgage and lending institutions in this country are not prepared to make the funds available, then it is the duty of the government to make them available. I am not talking about 1 per cent money; I am not talking about 2 per cent money. If it costs the government 3 per cent then we will charge 3 per cent, and one quarter per cent to cover the overhead. I am not asking for a subsidy from the government or from anyone else. All I suggest is that there is a real and vital problem which concerns all of us, and which is not receiving the attention it deserves.
I think the government will hear a great deal more about housing in the days ahead. Up to the present time they have done about as well as could be expected, and a great deal when measured by any yardstick. As I have suggested, I think the mortgage and trust companies are making this an opportunity to increase their mortgage rates. I am asking the minister now, as I asked him a year ago and as I have repeated since then, to see that mortgage money is made available to credit-worthy Canadians. I am glad there are members on the other side now joining me in that appeal; I hope that we shall have some success.

Mr. Speaker, we have heard this afternoon speeches by two Toronto members, both Liberals, and two speeches more dissimilar could scarcely be heard in this house on a single afternoon. I want to say that I agree in the main with the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) rather than with the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Hunter). Indeed I think the hon. member for Spadina sits in the wrong place in the house. As a matter of fact I think he should be sitting with us, because so often his ideas are in tune with what we are thinking in this corner of the house.
Be that as it may, I want to say that I agree. As a matter of fact the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), who intended to speak on this matter this afternoon, left me a few clippings on his desk when he went out which confirm what the hon. member for Spadina said. This clipping is from the Ottawa Journal of May 23, 1952, and reports what Mr. Mansur had said before the banking and commerce committee the day previous. This reads:
Dealing with another aspect of construction financing, Mr. Mansur indicated that the CMHC and

National Housing Act
Canada's commercial lending institutions do not see eye to eye on mortgage-loan policy.
He said the short amortization period is the "holy cow" of the lending institution. They were more interested in protecting their loans than in maintaining a "flexible and progressive policy.''
Lending institutions did not want to make mortgage loans running for more than 20 years. The CMHC made loans up to 30 years depending on the borrower's ability to repay.
But there was a limit on the amount of money the CMHC had available for lending purposes. If lending institutions would broaden their policies, he added in an interview, the amount of housebuilding in Canada might increase.
That is exactly what my hon. friend has in mind, as well as the pressure to increase mortgage rates.
There is another aspect of this matter about which I should like to talk briefly this afternoon because I think it is an important one. I agree with what was said earlier as to the necessity of building homes on serviced land. The hon. member for Parkdale did not approve of the kind of housing that is under way in Great Britain. As a matter of fact, the stress in the early days after the war was on the building of permanent rather than temporary dwellings; but there is one thing about the houses being built in that country and that is that they insist on them being built on serviced land. There must be water, there must be sewer facilities, there must be drainage and so on. Here that is not demanded, either by Central Mortgage and Housing or the municipalities in which the buildings are to be built.
The hon. member for Parkdale indicated this afternoon what private enterprise could do in this regard. I have on my desk a letter which was sent out by the national house builders' association, with headquarters at 21 King street east, Toronto. This letter was provoked by a news release dated November 26 by the Department of Resources and Development announcing Canada's largest subsidized housing project to date at Saint John, New Brunswick, which is to contain 200 family units and cost about $1,900,000. This letter then goes on to say:
Why is the Canadian government so vigorously promoting subsidized housing?
And again:
Public housing kills individual incentive.
And further down:
Private enterprise has made Canada great and has done a job second to none in the field of housing. Are you for socialistic subsidized housing or private enterprise? Give us legislation designed for home owners on a basis which rewards initiative and pride of ownership.
What is to prevent them exercising their initiative now? There is no law against the building of homes under free enterprise. It is because free enterprise has failed to
rMr. Coldwell.l
produce the homes that are needed that we have had to have a housing act and have had to consider legislation of this description over the last several years. There is nothing to prevent them if they want to engage in building houses under private enterprise. They can go ahead, and I think everybody will be pleased to see more houses being built. There was a quotation which I saw the other day in a popular magazine reading as follows:
Many people consider things a government does for them to be social progress but they regard the things government does for others as socialism.
That is precisely the tenor of this letter sent out by the house builders' association. One of the factors militating against the purchase of homes in this country was referred to by Mr. Mansur on the date I have already given and is reported in the same article, and I quote:
Turning to the question of builders' loans. Mr. Mansur said at one point, ''there are exceptions but most builders are interested in obtaining as large a profit on each house as possible.
''For example, one builder told me recently that our lending value pattern was not suitable to his building program, as he preferred to build only four or five modest houses a year with a profit of $2,800 on each.
"Our lending values do not envision such a large profit."
I have great respect for many builders in this country who have tried to do a decent job at a decent price, but there are some organizations, there are some builders and there are some large contractors who are out to make a killing as far as housing is concerned. They know what is perfectly true, that there is a shortage of houses in Canada. I am not going to enter into an argument with the hon. member for Parkdale as to whether there is a backlog of 750,000, 500,000, 200,000 or, in his district, 27,000 houses; I am not talking about that as I do not know what the figures really are, but I do know that rents have skyrocketed because of the demand for housing.
I do know that there is a great deal of overcrowding in many of our towns and cities from Vancouver to Halifax. I do know that a great many people are occupying crowded rooms in obsolescent buildings and living under conditions that do not reflect much credit on this country or, may I say, on the various governments of this country.
I mentioned a year ago that I had had some personal knowledge of the building of a home in this city by one of these contractors. Ever since this particular house has been occupied it has been found that things were scamped, things were improperly done and considerable money has had to be spent doing things that the contractor should have done in the

first instance. When they came to look at the drainage around the foundation they found that it had not been drained. They had to get another contractor to put in the drainage pipes. This particular contractor built a lot of houses in this city. On the first evening that one young couple inhabited one of these homes the man decided to have a bath. He filled the tub, had his bath and pulled out the plug-and the water went into the living room below. Yet that was the contractor who was awarded or was going to be awarded a contract last fall to build housing for the government to the tune of $1,500,000.
I think one of the matters the government should carefully review is that of inspection. It is left to the lending institutions, and I happen to know that one of the lending institutions in that very area, when they were asked about the manner in which the houses had been built, wrote and said that was no concern of theirs; that all they were concerned about was the mortgage and the payment of the mortgage.
If that is the attitude of some of the lending institutions then I think it is high time we said to the minister that we should have our own inspection service and inspect the homes with people who are qualified, people who can do a job and make an inspection. At the same time I think we should see to it that these inspectors who are put on the job are not given any special concession by the contractor on the houses they themselves buy or inhabit. I believe that happens in some cases.
I think the time at least has come when we, as members of parliament, should try to protect the people who are trying to build homes in this country in which to live. As far as I know, no satisfactory disposition has been made of the complaints. The down payment has been made, the mortgage is on, and in each case the people who occupy these homes have an obligation to pay and I do not know what their remedy is. I know that in one particular case where people went into a home, after watching it being built, they had to pay over $300 to fix the foundation and do various things that the contractor did not do. He was one of the big contractors in this city and I feel inclined to put his name on Hansard.
Name him.

The Campeau Construction Company of this city, a firm which is doing quite a lot of building here, and jerry-building at that. I say to the minister that if we are going to encourage people to buy homes then we should see to it that they are protected by proper inspection. The builders may say that is an interference with private enterprise, but I say it is not. They can build all the houses
National Housing Act
they wish. We are doing a great deal for the builders and for the lending institutions in giving these guarantees to them, and I think it is only fair to ask the lending institutions and the building organization to give a square deal to the people of Canada and to those who must obtain homes at this time in this city.

Mr. Speaker, I am just going to speak briefly on this subject and on three or four points which have not, in my opinion, been adequately covered by the act. There is first of all the problem of providing serviced land in large and small municipalities. Second, there is the question of municipal taxation which so seriously affects the construction of houses. Third, there is the insecurity of the people who already have houses and are paying for them.
The problem of serviced land is one of the most vital and one of the most serious questions we face today. In the municipality in which I live, and in the five municipalities which constitute the riding which I represent, the preparation of an acre of land costs in the neighbourhood of $10,000, that is to provide all the physical services and the schools. The figure covers the process of bringing raw land to the point where it is properly serviced land with school facilities. If you build houses at the density of five per acre, it means you have a capital cost of approximately $2,000 per lot before the first shovelful of earth is taken out and construction begins.
This is a problem, Mr. Speaker, which I believe the federal government is doing nothing to solve. The government realize the problem and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation realize the problem, but they do not realize the immensity of the problem. They are just toying with its solution.
Around Toronto there is an extremely dense population and very rapid growth. The question of providing serviced land is almost driving the municipalities into-I will not say receivership, but it is certainly driving them into straitened circumstances; and the municipality in which I live must put a prohibition on any further housing development because that municipality cannot afford to provide serviced land. It cannot afford to provide schools, sewers, streets and other things without imposing a municipal tax burden on the people already living there which would make home owning so expensive that it would destroy the security and equity in the homes already built. It is a situation which is fairly general in or around Toronto, and I imagine it is fairly general around all the major metropolitan districts in Canada today.
4480	HOUSE OF
National Housing Act
The solution of the provision of serviced land must receive more attention than it has under this bill. I have a suggestion-made on my own account, and I am not speaking for the party-and I would like to hear some discussion or criticism of it. My suggestion is that municipalities should be allowed to issue tax-free bonds. I realize that is heresy, but there must be some method by which municipalities can obtain more funds to provide serviced land and schools. I do not agree that municipalities should have their own taxing powers enlarged or that they should be allowed to go back into the income tax field or anything of that nature. In my opinion that would be a retrogressive step; but the municipalities must be able to provide this serviced land, without penalizing the people already living within their boundaries.
In rapid growth areas there is an unbalance of industry as compared with domestic construction. The higher the percentage of domestic construction and the lower the percentage of industry, the more likely you are to have a municipality in financial difficulties. That is something, of course, which the provinces must consider when more money is borrowed by municipalities. What the proper percentage is, I do not know. Certainly in the dormitory suburbs which have been created around many of our metropolitan areas, the percentage of domestic construction to industry is away out of line. All this means that a man who already has a house, who can meet the mortgage payments, finds that with the ever-increasing burden of municipal taxation his cost of home ownership is constantly increasing, and as his annual cost of home ownership increases his security in his home decreases.
I consider that one of the most dangerous situations which we have to face in Canada today, particularly in industrial centres.
