If there should be a temporary period of unemployment in these centres, if industry were to lay off the men for a few months, you would find that with these tremendous annual costs of home ownership a man would be deprived of his interest in his home. Fortunately that is something which we have not had to face as yet. However, should there be a slight recession in industry, should there be even a 10 or 15 per cent recession, we are going to find that a large number of people, who are today just getting by, will be in extremely difficult circumstances. It is on behalf of those people that I wish to appeal to the government in connection with this question of municipal taxation which is, in turn, based partially upon the provision of serviced land.


There is one other problem with which I should like to deal very briefly. I have mentioned it in this house before. It is the question of providing mortgage money for homes built in areas which are not strictly covered by the act. Today a lot of men are building their own homes, particularly in the industrial areas, or they are assisting in the construction of their own homes. They are working on the week ends and at nights, and a great deal of work is being done by these people or their friends. Frequently they build houses which are not included in any major plan or housing development, although they are within areas earmarked for residential construction.
What happens to these men is that they find themselves outside the scope of this act. Instead of being able to borrow money through the provisions of the act or through a regular lending institution, they have to go to private sources for their mortgages. Here they are penalized. There have been numerous cases brought to me where a man has asked for a mortgage of, shall we say, $5,000 or $6,000, and has been forced to sign a mortgage for $500 to $1,500 more in order to obtain the mortgage he desired. This is quite legal, but it seems to me that the provisions of this act should be broadened in such a way as to stop this practice, as it is evil and pernicious.
I want to say one further word about planning. The municipality which is properly planned will prevent uneconomic housing developments. There are many municipalities which are just allowed to grow like Topsy, and in those municipalities there is a vicious type of development known as the "ribbon development". In other words, a farmer will sell off the front 100 or 150 feet along the highway. A strip of houses is built, but the farmer maintains his farm. These houses immediately require services. They may get by for three or four years, but eventually they require schools because the school population goes up by leaps and bounds. Sewers and all the other services are required before very long. This ribbon type of development is the most uneconomical type possible, because instead of having a compact housing development easily serviced you have a long ribbon of houses which require lengthy and very costly services.
What happens then? Taxation on the farms and on the buildings in this municipality increases astronomically, destroying the value of the land which has been so developed. So far as I can see nothing has been said in this act about town planning. I should like to see the money provided only in municipalities which are adequately planned. With the present type of ribbon development, not only

are we destroying the value of the land so developed but we are increasing the cost of highways. We are making the whole highway problem much more acute, and we are not producing economically the houses which are needed. So long as things of this sort continue we are going to have housing uneconomically produced, and we are going to have an increasingly difficult problem of municipal financing.
I have mentioned the three points that I felt might be considered. I have suggested municipal taxation being allowed as a deduction from income for tax purposes, and mortgage payments also being allowed as a deduction from income. I do so again. I believe all these things should be studied. The reason for our housing problem is that we are building uneconomically, and we are placing on the people least able to bear it the burden of maintaining domestic structures. Not only that, but because of our high incidence of municipal taxation we are increasing the burden today on people whose security depends on an hourly wage. If for any reason that hourly wage is suspended, if there is a slight recession or if there is any degree of unemployment, we are going to find that there will be an avalanche of defalcations on mortgage payments, and a staggering growth of tax arrears.
I lived through the years of the thirties when municipalities found it extremely difficult to pay their way and when many went into receivership and had to make arrangements for their funded debt. I lived through that period and saw what it meant to people whose homes were virtually taken away from them because they were unable to meet the payments. Having seen that, I feel that unless something is done to ease municipal taxation on the home owner, we are likely to create with respect to the home owner a debt structure which will result in a desperate situation similar to that which was created during the period of unemployment in the early thirties.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to this debate. If anyone had said what I am going to say, I would not have stood up. I agree with many others that if there was any possibility of solving the housing problem under the present mechanics, the present minister would have done so. But I am convinced that, with the machinery with which he has to work, he is not going to solve that problem.
In listening to this debate what I am concerned about is this. What is the policy of the different groups in the house with regard to getting homes for the Canadian people?
National Housing Act
Everybody makes a speech, goes over the disability and diagnoses the disease, but does not prescribe anything to effect a cure, with the exception of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy).
Don't forget the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston).
I was not in the chamber when he spoke, but if he prescribed anything I will have to read his speech to find out what it was.
Yes. He laid down part of our policy; and it was a good one, too.

The hon. member for York South made a criticism of the present government's policy. But in addition to that he moved an amendment. In that amendment he made three suggestions, one with regard to making money more readily available, one with regard to providing a lower interest rate and providing a subsidy, and he also suggested that the government's agency, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, should go into a low-rental program in order to provide homes for those who perhaps will never be able to buy them.
As far as the C.C.F. are concerned, that is our policy. That is the thing we would do- and it is the thing the government is not doing-if we had the responsibility of solving the problem. On the other hand, I listened with a great deal of interest to the spokesmen for the Progressive Conservative party. They diagnosed the disability and they criticized the government; but if I heard them aright, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) particularly, they put on the record part of a statement by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), which was to the effect that he would call a dominion-provincial conference and find out what could be done in order to solve the problem. That is their policy: call a dominion-provincial conference.
As I understand it, the government's policy is to farm out money to the lending agencies at 2 or 2J per cent and they in turn-
3J per cent.
All right, 3f per cent; and the lending agency farms it out to those who wish to purchase a home, at 5i per cent.
Under that arrangement the interest rate would be close to 5J per cent.

That is what I said. That is the government policy. In that way they think they are going to get homes built. We have had that system operating since the end of the war, improving it a little bit as we went along but at the same time stepping up interest rates. However, it has not provided a solution.

National Housing Act
In this debate the hon. member for Park-dale (Mr. Hunter) mentioned this backlog of housing. Figures of that kind are only an estimate, anyway. The figures that were put on record by the hon. member for York South were an estimate that was made by a government committee-the Curtis committee-at the end of 1952. These things are only estimates; there is nothing firm about them.
The second criticism the hon. member for Parkdale had to make of what the hon. member for York South said was "Oh, it is socialist thinking". That is an old story. Nobody pays much attention to that sort of thing any more because it is worn out. I think most of the members of the C.C.F. across the country -including those in the one province in which there is a C.C.F. government-have demonstrated to the Canadian people that, regardless of the tags the chamber of commerce wants to hang on them in order to scare the Canadian people, they are fair and reasonable people and good Canadians. Hence that particular angle is not productive of much good at this time.
He stated that if the government were to provide subsidies and low-rental housing in the manner suggested by the hon. member for York South, it would mean a great increase in taxation. That is another bogeyman they are throwing around. The fact of the matter is that what the hon. member for York South suggested was not the government going out and borrowing money from the banks, the trust companies or the insurance companies, but using the agency that was created by the government for the purpose of providing money of this kind for capital expenditures on projects that are or will be self-liquidating. The hon. member for York South suggested the use of the Bank of Canada to make that money directly available to the people who would use it to provide houses. If you want to charge 2 per cent, all right; but you could actually do it through the Bank of Canada without charging any interest or imposing any new taxation on the Canadian people.
The fact of the matter is that the arrangement that is supported by the hon. member for Parkdale would add to the burden of the Canadian taxpayer, because if you farmed the money out to the lending institutions at 3J per cent they would in turn sell it to the home buyer at 5J per cent, which would be a subsidy to the insurance companies in that field, and it is paid by the Canadian taxpayers.
Five o'clock.

Mr. Speaker calls order in this house. The hon. member for Parkdale is away off base on this question. Actually he opposes what would relieve the taxpayers of Canada
l Mr. Gillis.]
of the subsidy now paid to the lending institutions, and supports a device used now to try to provide housing that actually means a burden to the Canadian taxpayers. Therefore I suggest that he take another look at the proposition.
In the matter of a subsidy generally, the Canadian government is pretty well committed to the principle. Are you getting uneasy, Mr. Speaker?
It is five o'clock. Has the hon. member almost completed his remarks?
No.
Well, it will be necessary for me to call it five o'clock.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, March 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Adamson for the second reading of Bill No. 224, to amend the Canada Elections Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: AMENDMENT REGARDING POLL CLERKS AND ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
This bill was debated by the mover on the last occasion that it came before the house and I moved the adjournment of the debate, promising at that time to give consideration to the three propositions contained in the bill. I have consulted with the chief electoral officer and he has reminded me that what I said on that occasion was slightly incorrect.
The proposals contained in the bill have been discussed on two previous occasions by committees of this house, and on each occasion the committee decided that they ought not to adopt the proposal made by my hon. friend.
Then, as to the other point, namely the question of the town of Atikokan being provided with an advance poll, I am informed that that was done in 1949, though it does not appear in the list as shown at the back of the Dominion Elections Act.
Then, finally, as to the suggestion that advance polls could be established in townships in addition to incorporated cities and towns, that matter was considered by the committees studying this act two and three years ago. The general feeling was not to have very many advance polls, but to restrict them as much as could be done within the limits of the act, which required that the

opinion of the chief electoral officer be obtained on whether there was likely to be a certain number of votes cast, or there had been on previous occasions.
For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, we feel that at least for the time being we should not agree to this bill, but we will assure the hon. member that the elections act committee will, after the forthcoming election, do what it always does, namely review the act in the light of the experience gained on that occasion, and all these questions can be discussed then.

subtopic: AMENDMENT REGARDING POLL CLERKS AND ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: AMENDMENT REGARDING POLL CLERKS AND ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext: If the hon. member speaks now he will close the debate.

subtopic: AMENDMENT REGARDING POLL CLERKS AND ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
The reason I introduced this bill was to bring to the attention of the house a system under which on election day a great number of persons are employed whose usefulness is perhaps questionable. I refer to the candidates' agents at the polls. No candidate will wish to allow a poll-at least that has been my experience and the experience of all candidates to whom I have talked-to go without having an agent there to observe the conduct of the operation of the poll on polling day. Both the deputy returning officer and the poll clerk are representatives of the government in power, appointed by the government in power and on a political basis. Therefore a member of any opposition party who wishes to see that his party's interests are properly served will have to provide at each poll persons who are known as outside and inside scrutineers. My purpose in bringing this amendment to the house was to see if we could not get around this business of providing scrutineers on election day.
In an average riding there will be probably 125 to 150 polls, and sometimes more. The cost involved in providing scrutineers may run as high as $1,000 or even more on election today. It seemed to me that was an unnecessary and unfair cost to be borne by the candidate of an opposition party. For that reason I introduced the bill. It has been debated, and I have the debates here. Mr. MacNicol, chairman of the opposition group considering the elections act, introduced it twice in committee. It was actually debated once and the debates are printed in the transcripts of proceedings of that committee for 1938. It had also been debated before that.
I have read carefully the debates on this question. There is nothing in them which persuades me in any way that the move would not be a good one. The amendment was voted down twice before on a strictly
Canada Elections Act
party division in committee, the three opposition members voting in favour and the seven government members voting against.
I think the amendment is desirable, and that it would save a large sum of money to all candidates, particularly those in urban constituencies. It follows the practice of having urban enumerators chosen by the parties obtaining the highest and second highest number of votes at the last preceding election. The principle has been admitted in another part of the act. The fact that the government does not see fit to consider it now is just one further indication that the matter is being considered on a party basis. I very much regret the government's decision.
We come now to the question of the revised statutes, and the insertion of the word "township". Canada has developed to the point today where townships have become major municipalities. Of the two townships in the constituency of York West, one has something over 75,000 people and the other has 110,000 or 120,000. Both are major cities, and would be so considered. Because they are not mentioned specifically in the act there cannot be an advance poll, except in respect of those townships so specifically mentioned. This includes the townships of North York, York and, I believe, Scarboro. Other townships do not have the benefit of this provision. For example the township of Etobicoke, with a population of more than 75,000 at the present time, has no provision whatsoever for an advance poll. It means that any resident in this community would have to go elsewhere to vote, if he was going to be absent on election day.
The reason for having advance polls was to provide certain people engaged in travelling, including commercial travellers, railway workers and others whose duties kept them away from their ridings on election day, with an opportunity to cast their ballots during the three or four preceding days. I believe this was a wise provision.
However, particularly if there is a summer election, there will be thousands of people, including travellers as well as others whose work would take them out of their home constituencies, who will be away from their homes on any particular day. Their business will take them away. The fact that in many cases they will have moved their families to summer cottages will remove them from the areas in which they would poll their votes. To deny them an advance poll will cause great hardship to a large number of constituents. It would have been at least a gesture if the government had seen its way clear to accept this one small amendment.
4484	HOUSE OF
National Housing Act
It would not have caused any difficulty whatsoever in the operation of the legislation if the word "township" were included in the act as it now stands.
If there is to be a summer election thousands of people will be deliberately disfranchised because they will be travelling or, for other reasons, will be away. If there is no provision for an advance poll in a township such as Etobicoke there will be a very serious dislocation of polling, and many thousands of people in my opinion will be disfranchised. The thing is pernicious and indefensible, and I believe deliberate. I very much regret the government's intractable attitude.

speechtext: The hour for private and public bills having expired, the house will resume the business interrupted at five o'clock.
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Winters for the second reading of Bill No. 339, to amend the National Housing Act, 1944.

Mr. Speaker, when you called it five o'clock I was making some comments on the matter of housing, and saying that the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Hunter) was considerably astray in his assertion that what had been recommended in an amendment by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), which was subsequently ruled out of order, would have added a burden to the taxpayers of Canada. No one has any objection to the insurance companies or the lending institutions investing the policyholders' money. That was one criticism made by the hon. member for Parkdale. They are entirely free to do that regardless of what the government may be doing in the way of providing housing. What we do object to is that at the present time the government is
[Mr. Adamson.)

subsidizing the insurance companies and in addition is guaranteeing them against any losses they may encounter in this field.
Another thing I object to particularly is that the insurance companies are not providing housing where it is needed. Their policy is to make an economic survey, and they are prepared to allocate a certain amount of money for the building of homes in those sections which show a bright future. The hon. member for Parkdale and others referred to this matter of serviced land, and in my opinion that problem arises out of the policy pursued by the lending institutions and by industrial corporations across this country in the centralization of industry in a couple of provinces. That means that the lending institutions are centralizing their building programs around the industries in Ontario and Quebec, with the result that they are running out of serviced land.
Not long ago I read a speech made by the mayor of Toronto at a convention, in which he pointed out that the burden upon the municipalities of this province was becoming unbearable because of the influx of people. The providing of schools and other services for these additional people was becoming such a problem that the governments would have to take a look at it very soon. I agree with him. The criticism that serviced land is not available arises out of the policy pursued in the centralization of industry and the building of cities around that centralized empire.
I am also concerned about the policies of the contending parties. I understand the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) made some constructive suggestions, and I am sorry I did not hear him. We have recommended procedures that would be workable if the government would adopt them. In my opinion the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) stated the official position of the Conservative party. He read into the record a statement made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) that they would call a dominion-provincial conference. The hon. member was very emphatic about this business of free enterprise. As far as I am concerned there is no such thing on this North American continent. It is neither free nor is it enterprise. At one time a man would go out and risk his money. He would build an industry and take his chance. But there is no risk capital any longer; it has to be guaranteed certain rates of interest, and against loss.

Did you ever buy any oil
stocks?

You had better be careful. If the war in Korea ends, away go your stocks. The hon. member for Broadview was down in Saint John, New Brunswick, recently and had something to say about housing. I have in my hand a clipping from the Saint John Loyalist of April 25, 1953, so it is right up to date.
Everything down there is up to date.

The heading of this article is "Rental Scheme 'Cockeyed'; Urge Change on Commission." Apparently they are setting up some kind of commission to provide low rental housing and the hon. member was quite critical of it. I had better put his own words on the record. I am doing this because I come from the maritimes and when they see this description of the low rental housing available in Ottawa as set out in this article I will have to answer some questions when I go back. The article reads:
Private enterprise in Ottawa is building multiple-unit housing to rent at $50 per month, without subsidy, George Hees, M.P., said while in Saint John. He discussed housing programs after hearing representations of Mr. Leo McNulty and Mrs. Vera Dorey.
Then he went on further:
According to the Toronto M.P. the present plan "sounds cockeyed" and is evidently an "unsound proposition."
He offered to forward plans of the Ottawa private enterprise plan, and said that the builders would invite inspection by a delegation from Saint John.
The article continues:
Mr. Hees said that the Ottawa project is brickfaced apartments, sound-resistant, with three bedrooms, kitchen, dining room, staircase and cellar. During the first year, he said, each head of a household agrees to work one hour per week about the grounds.
When I read that I said to myself, "Where do you get that kind of accommodation in Ottawa for $50 a month?" I have been coming to this city for the last 13 years, and I began to think that perhaps I had not been checking up closely. So I called some friends of mine who live in the city, one just down here on Metcalfe street. He has a little kitchen, a bathroom and sitting room with a pull-out couch. I asked him what he paid for that accommodation and he told me he paid $80 a month. I said, "You do not know about the sanctuary described by the hon. member for Broadview."
So I called another party who I thought was living in accommodation more like that described by the hon. member for Broadview. This party told me that he was living in an old house and that they had had to do one-half of the decorating themselves. They had two bedrooms, a sitting
National Housing Act
room and kitchen, yet were paying $150 a month for that accommodation in an old house.
I wonder if I could set the hon. member for Cape Breton South right and say a few words here as to what I actually said?

Will you wait until I am
finished, and then you can make another speech.
I just wanted to set you right on what I said.
I am not saying that the report in the paper is right.
I just want to set the record right.

You can do that later. When I go back to my riding and meet the people there they will say, "What is the idea? We are paying terrible rents down here and yet you fellows in Ottawa can get this accommodation for $50 a month. How is it that you can provide that kind of accommodation in Ottawa for $50 a month?" I can reply that it is not correct but they will tell me that they read the statement by the hon. member from Toronto and I should have straightened it out before I came home. That is exactly what I am doing. I am trying to save myself a lot of questions when I get back home.
This party was paying $150 a month. The accommodation is not as good as the member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) describes. It is not brick-faced, with three bedrooms, kitchen, staircase and so on, for $50 a month. I trust that when the hon. member for Broadview gets a chance he will put on the record where in this city one can find that kind of accommodation provided now by private enterprise.
You know, Mr. Speaker, "private enterprise" is a slogan that has become badly overworked. Chambers of commerce, boards of trade and all agencies of that kind who are a bit afraid that someone may be getting around to doing a little planning in the economy, have built up a lot of fears and apprehensions in the minds of many people. That slogan has become overworked in the minds of people; and if it could have solved the problems of the world there has been ample of time over the centuries. We have been following that kind of system and we have developed wars, devastation, misery and poverty and have not learned to do very much about them.
When I look at plants like the one at Chalk River, and the development of science

today, I think how wonderful the brain of man is with respect to the things he can devise. However, he has never learned how to distribute bread and to provide a place for people to sleep. It is rather shocking to think about the matter in that way because it adds up to the fact that slogans do not solve anything, and that you must have people who really want	to	do	something.
We are all striving to obtain houses for the average person in this country.

As I have already spoken, could I set	the record straight	at	this	point? Iknow	I am not allowed	to	make another
speech.
Hear, hear.
But I want to correct the points.

We will	be	in	committee
shortly.

I would suggest that the hon. member wait until we do get into committee because there may be some things I would like to say on the point and I too am debarred from speaking until I close the debate.

I do not want to be discourteous to the hon. member, but I want to finish what I have to say. I shall boil it down because I know every member of the house could give a long talk on the subject before us.
I wish to say a word about the remarks of the hon. member for Parkdale regarding the backlog of houses and the difference in figures. As I said before, the figures are only estimates. The Canadian Congress of Labour met the government on March 6, 1953, and presented a brief. The Canadian Congress of Labour represents a large group of people in this country; they meet year by year and hammer out a program that is to be presented to the government. That program is developed in all parts of the country by workingmen in their local units which come under the congress for legislative purposes. There is no guessing about, their presentation to the government on the matter because they maintain an excellent research department that works in that field, and they gather figures. I am going to quote a paragraph of their presentation because I think it answers the criticisms of the hon. member for Parkdale:
The congress has urged year after year that greater attention he given to the question of low rental housing. Official figures indicate that, by ;he end of the current year, there will be a backlog of 735,000 dwellings. For the most part, the houses which have been built since the war are far beyond the reach of the vast majority of Canadian families. The 1951 census showed that well over half of Canada's wage and salary earning families

were getting $2,500 per year or less. These people cannot afford even the kind of housing which is being built by limited-dividend companies under the National Housing Act. Section 35 of that act provides for subsidized low rental housing, but very little building has been done under this section. The initiative is left to local communities, but the government could and should do a great deal to stimulate local initiative and provincial co-operation in this field.
The shortage of materials is no longer an obstacle. The defence program will soon be tapering off to some extent, and a housing program on a large scale will be an excellent way to take up any slack in employment. Furthermore, the government's immigration program will make a bad situation worse, unless prompt and effective action is taken to provide subsidized low rental housing.
That is the position of the Canadian Congress of Labour, and that is the number of family units we are going to require by the end of 1953. I would just like to point out to the minister that all the juggling and patching we can do with the National Housing Act, with our present mechanics, is not going to give homes to a large section of the Canadian people.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) made his budget speech he pointed out that there were 137,000 families in this country whose income levels were below taxable brackets. The National Housing Act fixes what is called an economic unit, that is a home costing over $10,000, with a $3,000 down payment. The 137,000 families whose incomes are below taxable level will never be able to provide homes for themselves under present methods of financing and present costs. No one can dispute that. The average Canadian family numbers four, so you can multiply 137,000 by four to get the number of people who are "out" under any circumstances at present.
What is the answer? The answer is low rental housing. Those people cannot find places to live with the rents that are asked today, in the light of their incomes. That figure is not a guess; it is the figure given by the Minister of Finance when he made his budget speech. Low rental housing is the answer. Even if the minister's department wants to carry on building $10,000 units financed by insurance companies, subsidized by the taxpayers of Canada-and the profits of the organization are subsidized to the extent of about 2 per cent-I think the minister should consider putting Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation directly into low rental housing across the country in order to provide homes on a subsidized basis, because they will have to be subsidized. With incomes such as I have described these people cannot pay rent for any kind of accommodation that is half decent and, in

the final analysis, they are the people who produce the wealth of this country.
I could go on and on and on, but I shall leave it for the minister. If he is not prepared to accept all of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), I believe that serious consideration should be given to the matter of low rental housing.

Mr. Speaker, I would just like to say one word before the minister speaks. I know he wants to get the bill through, but he will have to be patient. I want to say a word, and I am not like the member for Broadview who says something in some other province where it may catch up with him only by mistake. The houses in British Columbia all have blinds on them now, so we have no worries in that connection.
The main objection, Mr. Speaker-and I have had very little experience with housing in my particular riding-is that we are unable to get loans on homes adjacent to small towns or villages. I do not think it is fair, and I do not think that it is the intention of the act that such should be the case. The minister may shake his head but I happen to know that it is a fact.
Possibly the reason for it is some inefficiency in his staff, and I can quite understand that if all of his staff carries on in the same manner as his head man. I can assure him that I can give him plenty of real estate men from my riding who will work for one-third the salary and do a far more efficient job than the present head of this staff, though I appreciate that possibly the present head is not able to give his best efforts to the position because of his health.
I understand that the staff has a spring floor on which to dance. I want to register my objection to this spring floor. I want to register my objection to what, in my opinion, is a great extravagance in constructing this building in which to conduct this business, while the government cannot find money to build homes for people. They can find money, however, to construct beautiful oak floors with springs under them for this hardworking staff to dance upon. It does not go down with me.
I want the minister to explain to me why it is that in the village of Abbotsford a man with a secure income is unable to secure a loan. The references are on file in the minister's department, just as they are in my office. I presume the only reason is that the gentleman in charge, who draws this big salary, stumbled over the spring floor in the dance hall and could not answer the question.
National Housing Act
I want the minister to tell me why these loans are not available in areas adjacent to villages or small towns.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Earlier today the proposals put forward by the C.C.F. with respect to housing were described by the hon. member for Parkdale as thought-provoking. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, that is what we have been trying to do for a great many years, namely to provoke the thinking of the government and of the people of Canada with respect to the social importance of this question of housing. It was obvious from the remarks made by the hon. member for Parkdale that he is one of those in whose thinking we have not made much of a dent, but it is to be noted that we have made some progress across the years.
We have reached the point in this country where it is recognized that even though those in other parties in this house may talk about this being a private enterprise country, nevertheless this is a field in which the community has had to accept some responsibility. This fact is attested by legislation such as the National Housing Act, which is being amended at the present time, and by the provisions for building homes for service personnel, as well as other steps which have been taken by various levels of government.
However, the plain fact of the matter is that when one looks at housing, particularly in many of the large cities in this country, and also in the small towns and rural areas, we find we have not yet begun to provide for the people of Canada as a whole the kind of housing to which they are entitled or the kind of housing which we are capable of producing at the present time.
We believe that private enterprise will not do that, and that the time has come when we must move in the direction suggested in the proposals contained in the amendment which was moved earlier today by my colleague the hon. member for York South. We believe that the necessary money to finance the building of homes should be lent directly by government institutions, such as the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, to the builder at a nominal rate of interest such as 2 per cent. We believe, furthermore, that with respect to the important question of low rental housing for those in the lower and middle income brackets, and for those who have to move about in connection with their work, subsidies should be made available directly to public housing authorities. We believe the time has come when public authorities, such as the Central Mortgage and

National Housing Act
Housing Corporation, must go directly into the construction of houses.
I would point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that perhaps the strongest indictment of so-called private enterprise in the debate today was made by a member on the Liberal side of the house. We have pointed out-and the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) joined us in expressing the same view-that to a large extent the present legislation seems to be designed not for the purpose of getting houses built but rather for the purpose of subsidizing the lending institutions and enabling them to make profit out of this business of building houses. Today the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) reminded us that these same lending institutions, which have enjoyed great benefit from this legislation, on at least one previous occasion staged what amounted to a strike. They made it known that they would not continue to cooperate under the provisions of the National Housing Act unless they were permitted to charge a higher rate of interest. It was because of that strike on the part of the lending institutions that the rate of interest on joint loans was increased some time ago to approximately 54 per cent.
Today that indictment has been levelled again at the same institutions by the hon. member for Spadina, who points out that these same institutions are again saying that there is only so much mortgage money to go around, that many projects will have to be postponed and that housing will have to share in that postponement. What are they doing but threatening once again to stage a sit-down strike unless they get another increase in the rate of interest?
That being the case, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the answer will have to be a little stronger than the suggestion made by the hon. member for Spadina. I sense that he is still hopeful that if the government takes a strong enough position, the lending institutions will co-operate with the government. I suggest we have to go further than that. The time has come when this government will have to consider the proposals put before this house by the members of this group, particularly as set out in the amendment suggested earlier today by the hon. member for York South. I suggest that the time has come when, for the building of homes, the necessary money has to be lent directly to the builders by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at an interest rate such as 2 per cent. I suggest, likewise, that for the construction of the large number of homes that we need for low rental projects, subsidies will have to be made directly to

local public housing authorities and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will itself have to go into the construction of houses.
I realize that ideas such as these are strange to the ears of a member like the hon. member for Parkdale. He stands up and says that is socialism; he says it is the sort of thing he would expect from the socialist members down in this part of the house. Since he has referred to us as a socialist group-a correct reference, may I say-I would just refer him to what I thought was an interesting though brief definition of socialism given not long ago by one who knows what it is all about, Right Hon. Herbert Morrison. He defined British socialism as "the assertion of the principle of social responsibility for matters which are properly of social concern". It is that principle which this group has been asserting in this House of Commons and in this country from the time it was organized.
We have made progress. We have been able to bring the thinking of the Canadian people along to a certain extent. There are many things that are recognized in Canada as being properly of social concern. Some of them are taken care of at the municipal level. Some of them, like the education of our children, are taken care of at the provincial level. But there are others-matters other than those which are already recognized-which we feel are of social concern; and housing, we contend, is one of them. We believe that the day will come, if mankind continues to make progress as we believe it to be our destiny, when the right to adequate housing, the right to a decent home for every child born in a country like Canada will be recognized just as clearly as is the right to education and the right of the people as a whole to the many services which we provide on a common basis.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that we are not set back at all by the arguments made by the hon. member for Parkdale but rather we are encouraged to keep proclaiming that principle that there are certain things which are properly of social concern and which should be matters of social responsibility. It is our contention that one of the most important matters of social concern in Canada is that of providing adequate housing. Private enterprise has demonstrated that it cannot measure up to that responsibility. Private enterprise has been given another indictment today by the hon. member for Spadina in the statement he made earlier. We are not surprised at that. Their interest in the National Housing Act is simply in getting what they can out of it.

I submit that there is no longer any point in trying to bring the lending institutions along or in trying to get them to co-operate. The time has come for the people of Canada as a whole, through their government-that body through which they can exercise social responsibility-to go more thoroughly and more directly into the field of housing. This is something that is extremely important to our people. If we want to make our way of life mean and continue to mean that glorious experience that we believe it to be, one of the most important matters for us to give attention to is the need for and the right to adequate, proper and decent housing for every Canadian family.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. F. Higgins (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with attention to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and I found his arguments to be extremely persuasive indeed. In fact, if I were not watching myself I would feel almost like the Irishman and say, "If I were not a Conservative, I should like to be a socialist"; but I dare not go as far as that.
We must realize that, in the world in which we live today, the greatest threat confronting us in the western world is communism. Frankly, I think one of the best ways to keep communism from the western world as we know it is to provide proper housing accommodation for the people who live in the western world. If one were to go not too far from here, namely to the great city of Montreal, I have been told by a reliable person, in whom I have implicit trust, that one would find 2,000 families each living in what I will not call it a house but will call one room. If 2,000 families are each living in one room, how many more people are living in little better accommodation in that great city?
The obvious thing that happens to families living in such accommodation as this. They constitute a fertile field for the promulgation of communist doctrine. I feel that the greatest indictment which can be levelled against this government-I am not talking of the minister himself but of this government-is that they have not faced up to this issue which has been confronting the people of Canada for some years past.
There is a good deal to be said for the motion-which I understand was ruled out of order-to provide cheaper money for the building of houses. I am not saying that it is necessary to have money as cheap as 2 per cent. But if it is necessary and money at 2 per cent is required-and apparently a study has been made of the matter-then the government should make provision for
National Housing Act
such money to be supplied. Money at that rate cannot be supplied by private industry at the present time. It is just as well for us to realize that fact. The last issue of government bonds was placed on the market at 3J per cent, if I am not mistaken. Having that fact in mind, how can we possibly ask private industry to subscribe to a housing program at 2 per cent?
Mr. Speaker, the matter gets back again to the question of whose job this is. Is it the government's job? Is it the province's job? Is it the municipality's job? Is it the people's job?
The individual.

The individual is right; and the individual is the government. I therefore think the buck is passed right back to this government, and that the government has fallen down on the job. Unless the government gives proper leadership in providing homes-decent homes that can be lived in; homes that can be paid for by the class of people who will use those homes, and who are earning the amount of money that it will make it possible for them to pay for them-then you will have a country that is going to be absolutely ready for the communist doctrine, or one in which the people are going to be receptive to this communist doctrine. We can talk all we like about outlawing communism in this country but unless we give people decent houses over their heads it will do no good.
For that reason-and I am not going against any statement that has been made by any member of our party-I see a great deal in the amendment that was not accepted in this house, but which was presented by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy). I must say that I am greatly in favour of providing housing for the people of this country, and I am sure that all the members of this house feel the same way. It is merely a question of deciding what is the proper way. In this particular case the government should and must give the lead.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Resources and Development):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,

National Housing Act
I shall be brief in winding up this very interesting debate on housing. I wish to thank all hon. members who participated for the contributions they made. It must be clear to all hon. members, judging by the varying approaches to the problem that have been expressed, just how complex housing is and how difficult it is to evolve a formula that would be satisfactory to everybody.
In opening the debate this morning for the official opposition the hon. member for Eglin-ton (Mr. Fleming) said, among other things, that in 1951 the government made an error, and that as a result of that error there was a great decrease in house building. He also added the strange reasoning that had we built more houses at that time rather than now, the cost to the home owners would be considerably less. He completely overlooked the fact that there was a Korean war on at that time and that parliament specifically expressed itself as being in favour of assigning top priority to the defence construction program and endorsed the government's policy that housing should take second place only to the defence construction program itself. It therefore became necessary to put both housing and defence construction into proper perspective. It was only because of certain action the government did take that there was not even keener competition for labour and materials in 1951, and that costs remained at the relatively low level to which my hon. friend referred.
Had the government not exercised a measure of control through its policies, as it did at that time, there would have been a great deal of confusion and perhaps the fears which were expressed at that time would have been realized. If we had not taken the measures we did a great many houses that were started would then not have been finished. We were anxious to see that the houses started were completed so the maximum possible number of Canadians would have roofs over their heads.
Dealing with housing is almost analogous to walking a tightrope, Mr. Speaker. One must maintain a proper balance. It is as though an engineer were working with an equation in which there were many variables, the main variables being materials, labour and mortgage money with its interest rate, amortization period and down payment, and the problem of serviced land. On the other hand, when thinking of a loan on a house it becomes necessary for the borrower and the lender alike to consider both the amount of the down payment on the one hand and the amount of the debt burden on the other.
Hon. members of the opposition today expressed the wish that the government

decrease the down payment. At the same time other hon. members expressed concern about the amount of the debt burden. Both show their concern for various aspects of the problem, and the difficulty is to find a middle course which will be satisfactory to the majority of Canadians. It was indicated by one member of the opposition that it would be desirable for the government to reduce the down payment to as low as 5 per cent.
I had a computation made of housing across Canada, and I found that as of September, 1952, the average estimated cost of a house in Canada, the whole of Canada, was $11,358. The lending value of the house was $10,695; the actual loan, $8,123; the down payment $3,235, which under a 20-year amortization period involves principal and interest of $654, with total gross debt service of $850. And assuming that gross debt service should not exceed 23 per cent of income, that debt service would require an income of $3,696. If the down payment were reduced to 5 per cent instead of 20 per cent as it is, the required income would increase from $3,696 to $4,409, the gross debt service would increase from $850 to $1,014.
The hon. members who expressed concern lest the gross debt service would be too high would certainly have ample evidence there to support their case. Therefore the problem is to maintain a reasonably low down payment on the one hand without increasing the debt service so as to become too great a burden for too many Canadians. On the other hand, it is a fact that most of the mortgage money available now is being taken upland if the down payment were decreased and more mortgage money put into each loan there would be a lesser number of houses built with the available money.
It has been suggested that government action should be taken to enable existing mortgage money to be lent at a lower rate of interest over a longer amortization period and with a lower down payment than would otherwise be the case. That is exactly what the government has done, Mr. Speaker, through the facilities of the National Housing Act. As hon. members know, were it not for the National Housing Act the interest rate would be, I am sure, at least 6 per cent through the conventional lending channels. With the guarantees of the National Housing Act, lending institutions lend their money on the joint arrangement at 5| per cent. The federal government advances its 25 per cent of the loan at 3f- per cent, with the result that the cost of the loan to the borrower is now at 51 per cent. The amortization, which would probably be of the order of ten years were it not for the federal

government's participation, under the terms of the National Housing Act on joint loans could be up to 30 years, most of them now being of the order of 20 years. Under the Insurance Act lending institutions are limited to mortgages of not more than 60 per cent of the lending value of the house; whereas with the federal government participation through the National Housing Act it is 80 per cent of the agreed sale price.
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) made quite a case today, as he has done before, in trying to persuade the government of the wisdom of having the interest rate reduced to 4 per cent or less. That is the figure he usually uses. Well, certainly the government wishes that it were possible to make money available at 4 per cent or even less. But the fact is that the only way money could be made available at 4 per cent would be for the government to take the money from the people of Canada and make it available at that figure. Any such approach as this would have the effect of driving out of the market at once the money being loaned by the lending institutions conventionally and through the facilities of the National Housing Act joint loan technique. That money last year amounted to $494 million.
Hon. members said here today that lending institutions are not interested in housing loans, and are diminishing their operations. In 1951 the amount of money lent on residential mortgages was $474 million. Last year it increased to $494 million. Lending institutions I think are doing a good job in meeting their obligation of making mortgage money available for residential construction. I think it is important as a matter of policy that the federal government should neither be the landlord of too many Canadians nor should it hold the mortgages for too many Canadian homes. And I would suggest to my hon. friend from Broadview that if he harbours any remote hope of ever sitting on this side of the house, he would regard it as a pretty poor legacy if this government were to leave any incoming government in the position of being the landlord of large numbers of Canadians, and holding the mortgages of a great many Canadian home owners.
This is a young country. It is a growing country. The bulk of its growth is ahead of it; and1 it would be a pretty poor policy at this time if the government were to step in and take the primary position in housing to the extent that most housing hereafter would be built in a direct way by the federal government.
A great deal was said today about the backlog in housing. It was estimated by the hon.
National Housing Act
member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) at
700.000	units and by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) to be of the order of 500,000. It was said by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Hunter), in what I considered to be an excellent speech today, that the size of the backlog in housing in this country is very difficult indeed to evaluate. I think it might be pretty rash to attempt to establish it with any degree of exactitude at all. But I have looked into this problem with some care, and I find the arithmetic being employed by those who discuss the quantitative aspect of the backlog today to be related to the Curtis report, and to be arrived at by adding net family formations and subtracting the number of new housing units completed.
It seems to me that the 1951 census figures give a more accurate picture of the present situation. That census figure as in June, 1951, showed that there were 3,287,000 families in Canada and that there were 3,423,000 occupied dwellings. In addition there were 456,000 non-family households. These figures indicate that some 320,000 families and households share accommodation, or about 9 per cent. Any calculation of a backlog of housing need, if it is to be a valid figure, would have to be adjusted upward by some proportion of the
169.000	dwellings lacking either toilet or bathing facilities.
A large number of these houses-and they are houses, by the census definition-lie in the outlying areas and on the fringes of our urban communities. However, I do not believe that each of these units would be immediately vacated were more modern units available. Nor do I believe that the apparent excess of
320.000	family and household groups in relation to the number of occupied dwellings are indeed all potential occupiers of new housing units. From time to time an effort has been made to determine the extent of what might be called voluntary, as against involuntary, multiple occupancy. No satisfactory figures have ever been developed, but it is the opinion of those who have worked on this problem that at least two-thirds of the multiple occupancy is voluntary, for social or economic reasons. There is the case of the mother and father who live with their children or vice versa. For census purposes they would be considered two separate families. Indeed, if either the mother or father lived with a son's family, these also would be considered families for census purposes.
Likewise, in the non-family household the sharing of a single unit by two people of no blood relation would be considered a multiple occupancy. I mention these instances to indicate that gross figures taken either from

National Housing Act
census returns or from projections of the figures suggested in the Curtis report are likely to give an impression of greater housing needs measured by multiple occupancy than is really the case.
I would like to be able to give the house a reasonable estimate of the multiple occupancy reflecting housing need which presently exists in Canada, but I do not think it is possible to produce such a figure. Most of its components contain a large measure of estimate. On a national scale the problem is in better balance than it is in the large urban centres, where we would all agree there is housing congestion and more housing units are required. On the other hand, taking the number of families and nonfamily household groups and comparing them with the number of existing dwellings, having subtracted the dwellings without modern facilities, bears little relation to the real backlog of housing needs. Based on the figures I have given and assuming that somewhat more than two-thirds of all multiple occupancy is voluntary, the backlog of housing needs would work out arithmetically at less than 100,000 units.
Hon. members might quite correctly say that this calculation has no regard for obsolescence and substandard housing. I readily agree that this is a factor, and that unfortunately some housing is so bad as to be almost uninhabitable. To the extent that this is the case corrective steps should be taken, and the bill is designed to help. But hon. members know, too, that nothing tends to be as permanent as temporary or substandard housing; and having full regard to the varying degrees of adequacy of existing accommodation it is a fact that there are few Canadians indeed who do not have a roof over their heads.
There is one point, however, which I think is worth making. The retirement of any backlog of housing is in large measure dependent upon the price at which such housing can be made available. The hon. member for York South made this point very clearly in his remarks at the time the resolution was being debated. If a large number of units were made available at $15 a month, then I believe they would attract families out of multiple occupancy in much greater degree than if units were being made available at $95 a month. I would agree with hon. members that there is a backlog of housing need, but probably only a fraction of the 500,000 to
700,000	units suggested in the debate on the resolution.
Before leaving the question of the need for housing by existing families and other household groups, I would like to remind hon.


members that the amount of housing built in any year to look after not only the backlog but current needs is largely dependent upon the amount of money which the Canadian family or household is willing to spend upon housing. The dominion bureau of statistics has produced a number of figures in recent years, and indeed the weighting for rent or equivalent in the new consumer price index as compared with the cost of living index shows that the Canadian families and households on the average are spending a much lesser percentage of their disposable income for housing than in the years prior to the war. It will be recalled that in the cost of living index the weighting for rental or its equivalent was 19 per cent, whereas in the new consumer price index the weighting is 15 per cent. Whether those changes result from a preference for consumer durables such as automobiles, television sets and so on, I do not know. Nevertheless it is the case that lesser amounts, as a proportion of the disposable income, are being spent for housing. This has and will continue to have an effect upon the volume of new housing which is built.
This afternoon various hon. members asked what could be done to meet this housing problem, and suggested that the government face up to it. I suggest that the government has faced up to the housing problem and I expressed the doubt this afternoon, which I restate tonight, that there is in any country housing legislation designed better to meet the needs of the people than is the National Housing Act. In a sense hon. members can have it just about any way they wish under the terms of that act. There is ample scope for private enterprise; there is ample opportunity for those with initiative to do something to house people who otherwise could not afford to house themselves.
It has been suggested that more vigour should go into publicizing section 35 of the National Housing Act and inducing municipalities to take advantage of it. I have literally gone up and down this country explaining to provincial governments, to municipal governments and to anyone who would listen that section 35 was on the statute books for those who wished to use it. Neither the federal government nor I can go to a municipality and tell them what they must or can do with respect to housing, but I repeat that section 35 is available to those Canadian municipalities and provincial governments who wish to use it. They will find us most receptive.
Real results are being achieved in attacking the problem of housing. I mentioned at the start of this debate that housing starts this year so far have been at a level surpassing even the high production figures of 1950.

New construction in Canada as of March 31, 1952 amounted to 23,445 housing units; as of March 31, 1953, there were 32,651 housing units under construction. I submit that there has been a substantial achievement on the part of all those in Canada who are contributing to the solution of a problem which obviously everybody in this house, and certainly the government, deems to be one of the most important in Canada.
I wonder if the minister would answer one question. I did not wish to interrupt him-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister has closed the debate and perhaps the hon. member could ask his question when we are in committee of the whole.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
On section 1-Part I.

There are two questions I should like to place before the minister. I listened with a great deal of interest to the debate which has taken place today and which I think has been both instructive and helpful. We are all agreed that the problem is a most difficult one. When the minister was closing the debate he stated that the government advances 25 per cent of the amount loaned for an ordinary home under the National Housing Act. Would he tell the committee why that could not be increased, say to 50 per cent, and what would be the effect of the government making a change of that kind in its policy. It seems to me that if the government were to provide 50 instead of 25 per cent as at present, that change would alter the whole picture.
After hearing the speeches made today I am of the opinion that one of the great difficulties about this problem is that the Canadian lending companies do not have sufficient money available to meet the requirements. I was very much struck by the speech of the hon. member for Spadina this afternoon, and I thought he spoke with great common sense and realism. It seems to me that is one of the big problems, that the lending companies do not have the money available to finance the building of the houses that the Canadian people need.
If that is the case then the government will certainly have to step in further. The building of homes in Canada should not be tied down to what money the lending companies can or will advance. Yet I think the minister's answer was based on that premise, that he could go no further than the lending companies were prepared to go.
68108-284J
National Housing Act
I suggest to him that if the government advanced 50 per cent instead of 25 per cent it would then be possible to call for a lower down payment, perhaps 10 per cent, and for a longer time in which to repay the loan. It is all very well to say that people can get money for houses, but take the case of a young couple who wish to buy a home. In many cases they simply cannot find the down payment of 20 per cent. I think the minister said tonight that the average down payment in Canada was $3,300. That amount of money simply cannot be found by the average young couple trying to buy a home. It cannot be found, either, by the older family of modest means who have decided to stop renting and build their own home. I am quite certain that there will have to be some provision for reducing the down payment required from people in that category. I am not worried at all about those people who have the money to finance a house. In most cases they do not need the National Housing Act. But these young couples and older people of modest: means need additional help provided under the laws of Canada.
There is a further difficulty in that lending companies are most reluctant to lend money on houses in districts which are not just as wealthy as the best districts in the community. A young couple might want to build in the type of district where the standards were not the highest, but the lending companies hesitate to grant a loan in that type of district. It seems to me that is one serious defect in the present legislation.
We are finding in Vancouver that where people are required to make a 20 per cent down payment and are unable to provide the cash themselves, they go to a real estate firm or a broker and arrange for a second mortgage. They have to pay a high rate of interest on this and probably have to take a discount; they may have to give the broker a reduction of $1,000 or $1,500 in the amount he pays. In other words, the mortgage may call for $3,000 but he would actually pay only $2,000. That sort of thing happens when people are unable to find the down payment.
The minister has said today that building supplies are plentiful in Canada, and this statement is confirmed by the booklet published by the Minister of Trade and Commerce entitled "Supply of building materials in Canada-Outlook 1953." In the introduction I find this sentence:
On the basis of the surveys made, it appears that the supplies of building materials in 1953 will be sufficient to permit completion of all the construction known to be planned for the year.
So there is no shortage of any supplies. The minister also said that labour would be plentiful for house building in 1953, and he

National Housing Act
intimated that cost of construction would be up about 3 per cent. In my opinion one of the main difficulties to be met is that of the large down payment. I would ask the minister why the government is unwilling, or whether the government is unwilling, to provide more than 25 per cent of the joint loans. If that change were made, what would the effect be in so far as reducing down payments is concerned? Also, what would be the effect in extending the time in which the money must be repaid?
I have two other questions but the minister might answer these questions first.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not want to curtail the discussion, and a general discussion of the amending bill is allowed on section 1; but I would not want a repetition of the debate which took place on second reading.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, that question is right on section 1.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When I rose I indicated my doubt that it would come within any clause of the amending bill. I was looking at the minister who is piloting the bill, and he seemed to agree with me. I do not want to enter into a procedural argument, but I would ask Iron, members for their co-operation. As hon. members know, on second reading only the amendments contained in the bill are to be discussed and the principle is to be adopted. However, there was a general discussion on housing, and there was no curtailment of that discussion. Now that we are in committee on the bill I would ask hon. members to keep in mind the fact that if there is to be a general discussion on section 1 it must be with respect to the amendments contained in the bill. It would be helpful, therefore, if those who know the bill better than I do would remain within its limits.

Mr. Chairman, I think what you have said is quite correct. There is nothing in the bill which would alter the relationship between the government's portion of the joint loans and the portion put up by the lending institutions. In this particular case, if it will not broaden the discussion, I might attempt to answer the question by saying that at the present moment construction of housing is in a pretty good state of balance when one has regard to the availability of serviced land on the one hand and the availability of mortgage money on the other, having in mind as well supplies of material and labour.
The situation could very easily get out of bounds. Inflationary tendencies have been contained with the result that although the cost of labour and material did increase somewhat last year, the prices of houses
[Mr. Green.l
remained substantially stable. If it should develop for example that more mortgage money was available than could be absorbed with construction as it is, still at a high level, inflationary pressures would be quickly felt and the price of houses would go up again. However, there are other considerations, and I might say that this is one of the things we have considered very carefully. It is something with respect to which anyone could venture an opinion and perhaps come up with an answer that would meet with his entire satisfaction and perhaps the satisfaction of other people.
If the government were to increase its contributions to joint loans by putting up another 25 per cent Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation would first have to get some $150 million additional. It could only be obtained by taxation at a time when the people of Canada have shown that they are not too anxious to have an additional burden of taxation put on them.
It might save that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Where? Not on your suggestions.

Another point has to do with administration. When a lending institution comes to the conclusion that it should invest mortgage money in a property it usually likes to invest a relatively large amount in that property and, thereby, cut down the amount of administration, rather than scattering their effort over a large number of properties. They prefer to concentrate for administrative purposes. One might say that desire was not an important factor, but it is a factor to the lending institutions and they prefer to operate that way.
There is another feature, which is that the bulk of loans in this country are still made outside the facilities of the National Housing Act. The government is not anxious to do anything which will discourage loans outside the National Housing Act because we desire to develop the greatest contribution to housing in this country. If operations through the National Housing Act were made too attractive in comparison with normal channels outside the housing act, it would simply impose burdens on the government and on the National Housing Act, and I feel that we would not achieve the desired results. We would simply be changing the weight of the effort from channels which are well established now to the channels under the National Housing Act.
Those are some of the factors which we have had to consider in arriving at the decision to leave the situation as it is now; and it is working very satisfactorily.

I am afraid the minister's answer is not very helpful. However, if that is the best he can do I guess we will have to be satisfied for the moment.
One other question has to do with the problem of the services to be provided by municipalities. Has the government given any thought to making use of the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act, which was passed in 1938? It is chapter 33 of the statutes of that year, and provides for allowances to municipalities for municipal improvements which are self-liquidating. The interest charged is 2 per cent. While that act was not drawn to meet the exact situation which we face today, I would like to know if it could not be used to help solve the problem. Probably there would have to be amendments to the act, but there you have the precedent of the dominion government making loans to the municipalities at the very low rate of 2 per cent. I understand that the act has not been used to any great extent. Some loans have been made, some millions of dollars advanced under the act; but it does seem to me that the act could be very helpful in solving this question of getting services installed by municipalities so that more homes could be built.
I should like to have the minister's reaction to that suggestion, and also to the suggestion that the municipalities should be freed of any sales tax, at least on materials that are used for installing water mains, sewage systems and public services of that kind. As I read the Excise Tax Act, it does not exempt most of these articles, and I should think it would be a great help to the municipalities in providing the necessary services for homes if some relief of that kind were given. I should like also to have an expression of opinion from the minister with regard to that suggestion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before the minister replies, and because of the wide debate which these two questions might suggest, I should like to ask hon. members if they give unanimous consent to have these two matters discussed at this time. If we go into the first matter of the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act, and the second matter of the remission of sales tax for the purpose of buying materials, I think we will be extending the debate. It is not that I want to curtail discussion, but if I allow these questions to be answered, further questions might be suggested to hon. members and we would have a debate on something other than the amendments that are provided in this bill.
I am in the hands of the committee, but I have asked for the co-operation of hon. members to stay within the limits of the dis-
National Housing Act
cussion offered by these amendments. Unless unanimous consent is given, I am afraid I shall have to declare that these questions should not be answered because the debate would be out of order.

I shall not press the question concerning the sales tax, but in so far as the other matter is concerned we have had today a discussion which has largely centred around two or three issues. One of these issues has been how the municipalities are going to provide water, sewage services and a lot of other services of that kind. At least some of the amendments in the bill are directed toward meeting that problem. I submit that my question concerning the use of the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act is quite in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

The hon. member argues that there was a wide discussion on second reading of the bill, and even at the resolution stage introducing this amending bill. The mere fact that wide latitude was allowed at those stages does not necessarily mean that the same latitude should be allowed throughout the remaining stages of the bill.
That is point No. 1. Point No. 2 is that if I correctly read the explanatory note for this bill, then it deals with matters that have to do with slum clearance, increasing the statutory appropriations under parts I and II, and so on. It would mean that all questions pertaining to housing generally in Canada, that is the rate of interest, the increase in loans, the matter of the down payment, town planning-to which reference was made by the hon. member for York West -ribbon line development, and so on, would be in order. Surely we are in order in dealing with such things as the down payment on housing, the interest payment and various things of that kind. clearance. I submit to Your Honour we should be entitled to ask questions about it.
